items.body:
*By Megan Sumeracki*

This semester, I’m teaching a hybrid class that only meets on Thursdays. Because of this, we have met every week up until this week. However, with Thanksgiving break, my students will have a two-week gap right at the end of the semester. We will return from Thanksgiving break in early December, with the final exam looming around the corner.

These are particularly extreme circumstances, and some students will only have a few days off this holiday. Still, it’s common to come back from Thanksgiving break to hear “I can’t remember.” Or, even more concerning, the “wait, when did we learn this?” question.

As a cognitive psychologist specializing in learning, I’m not overly concerned. It’s counterintuitive, but forgetting is actually an extremely important part of remembering. It’s easier to understand why when we consider how forgetting occurs over time, and how spaced practice works.

In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve *(1)*. He showed that forgetting tends to happen very rapidly at first, and then slows down. He also showed that spreading out repetitions was more efficient than massing them, or cramming. We know from a wealth of research in the last 140 years that spaced practice slows the rate of forgetting. This research has confirmed, many times over, that cramming does not work in the long run. Instead, spacing practice leads to much more durable long-term learning and remembering *(2)*.

Why does spacing help? When we review information after some time has passed, it has started to fade. When we revisit the information—or better yet, when we retrieve the information—it takes effort. That effort is sometimes called a desirable difficulty, and it helps produce durable learning *(3)*. Each time we successfully retrieve something, it becomes easier to retrieve the next time, and it is forgotten more slowly afterward. In other words, a little forgetting sets the stage for more durable remembering.

Having a break for Thanksgiving provides a natural space to let students forget a little bit, and then give them a boost upon returning. The figure below shows curves that illustrate the general pattern reported in research on forgetting (e.g., *1, 2* ).

These curves are a simulation, not real data. They illustrate the general pattern reported in research on forgetting and spacing (Ebbinghaus, 1885/1913; Cepeda et al., 2006): memories fade over time, retrieving them brings them back, and each retrieval slows forgetting. The specific values were chosen for illustration and are not predictions.

There are other benefits too. Spacing out practice shifts the context in which the material is being practiced, which may also help produce durable learning and remembering *(4)*. It is also important to take breaks in general. Stress can tax our cognitive resources and make it harder for us to retrieve what we know *(5, 6)*. Sleep also plays an important role in consolidating new memories. If the break provides opportunities to catch up on sleep and destress, it can be beneficial for learning upon return as well. See this post on [The Importance of Sleep for Memory and Cognition](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2016/7/14-1) and this post, [When Do the 6 Strategies for Effective Learning Work Best?](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2017/4/20-1)

Of course, there is a limit to how much space we should put in between review or retrieval attempts. If the space is too long, and the information is completely forgotten, then students may need to relearn it. Likely there will be savings in relearning—i.e., it won’t take as long to learn it again as it did the first time *(1)*. However, the benefits from spaced practice will likely be much less than they would have been, or possibly eliminated. The goal is to retrieve or at least review older material before it is completely forgotten to get the boost. Check out this post, [Optimizing Your Learning Schedule](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2018/7/5-1), to learn more about this.

## How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)

in Food & Drink , History , Technology | November 26th, 2026 Leave a Comment

-->

“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sen­sa­tion of eat­ing and drink­ing — is a strange and com­plex and com­pli­cat­ed thing,” writes New York Times food edi­tor Craig Clai­borne . “I am con­vinced that there are a mul­ti­tude of peo­ple (Amer­i­cans, most­ly, to judge by the peo­ple who buy TV din­ners and frozen piz­zas) who have no taste what­so­ev­er.” That col­umn was pub­lished almost exact­ly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such con­ve­nience-ori­ent­ed food prod­ucts had already enjoyed promi­nence in Amer­i­can life for two decades. Though it could hard­ly have made a dent in the pop­u­lar­i­ty of TV din­ners, Clai­borne’s typ­i­cal­ly waspish aside did draw a let­ter of objec­tion from one Ros­alie Levine of Lake­wood, Cal­i­for­nia.

“I live alone, I must con­trol my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV din­ner’s price “can­not pos­si­bly be bet­tered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready din­ner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to pre­pare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up after­ward.” While none of these advan­tages were acci­den­tal, the oft-told sto­ry of the con­cep­t’s emer­gence begins with a cor­po­rate cri­sis.

“In 1953, some­one at Swan­son colos­sal­ly mis­cal­cu­lat­ed the lev­el of the Amer­i­can appetite for Thanks­giv­ing turkey, leav­ing the com­pa­ny with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it . “Inspired by the trays of pre-pre­pared food served on air­lines,” Swan­son sales­man Ger­ry Thomas set the machin­ery in motion to pack­age the unwant­ed meat with gravy and sides like corn­bread and sweet pota­toes, ready for stock­ing in Amer­i­ca’s frozen-food aisles.

The fol­low­ing year, Swan­son sold ten mil­lion such “TV din­ners,” a name attrib­uted to both the shape of the box­es and the form of enter­tain­ment fam­i­lies tend­ed to enjoy while eat­ing the meals with­in. “In 1950, only 9 per­cent of U.S. house­holds had tele­vi­sion sets — but by 1955, the num­ber had risen to more than 64 per­cent, and by 1960, to more than 87 per­cent,” writes Kovie Biako­lo in a more recent Smith­son­ian piece . (Among the Smith­son­ian Insti­tu­tion’s hold­ings, inci­den­tal­ly, is an orig­i­nal Swan­son TV din­ner tray .) Anoth­er break­through came with the intro­duc­tion of microwave-safe trays, bring­ing total prepa­ra­tion time under ten min­utes. Dur­ing the COVID-19 pan­dem­ic, Amer­i­cans rekin­dled their love affair with frozen meals, “spend­ing near­ly 50 per­cent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

items.body:
**STUTTGART. „Vielfalt stärken – Zukunft gestalten“ lautete das Motto des Jahreskongresses Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026, zu dem am 26./27. November in der IHK Region Stuttgart rund 400 Ausbilder:innen, Schulleitungen und Lehrkräfte zusammenkamen.**

Dr. Christoph Franz, Dr. Benny Pock, Andrea Bosch, Dr. Jens Brandenburg und Andreas Deuschle beim Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

Mit **Andreas Deuschle, Staatssekretär im Ministerium für Kultus Baden-Württemberg**, wurde heute der Jahreskongress Berufliche Bildung (jakobb) 2026 in Stuttgart eröffnet. Deuschle vertrat Kultusminister Andreas Jung, der in diesem Jahr erstmals die Schirmherrschaft des Kongresses übernommen hat. Jung bezeichnete die berufliche Bildung kürzlich in einem Interview als „Flaggschiff“, „Aushängeschild“ und eine Basis des wirtschaftlichen Erfolges seines Bundeslandes. Entsprechend wurde auf die duale Ausbildung im Koalitionsvertrag von BÜNDNIS 90/DIE GRÜNEN und CDU ein besonderer Schwerpunkt gesetzt. Im Begrüßungsgespräch mit der stellvertretenden Hauptgeschäftsführerin der IHK Region Stuttgart, Andrea Bosch, ging es darum, wie das Kultusministerium dieses Vorhaben gemeinsam mit dem Wirtschaftsministerium in Schulen und Betrieben mit Leben füllen will. Deuschle betonte dabei, dass es gelte, „gemeinsam Perspektiven zu schaffen“.

**Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg**

Dass diese politische Zielsetzung nur gemeinsam gelingen kann, spiegelte das Teilnehmerfeld des jakobb 2026 wider: Als Plattform für die berufliche Bildung versammelt der Kongress einmal im Jahr alle Schlüsselakteure an einem Ort. Von der Berufsschullehrkraft bis zur Personalleitung mittelständischer und globaler Unternehmen nutzten die Entscheidungsträger den Austausch in Stuttgart, um Weichen für die Ausbildung von morgen zu stellen.

**Dr. Christoph Franz**, Vorsitzender des Berufsschullehrerverbands Baden-Württemberg (BLV), und Mitveranstalter des jakobb, zum Konzept: „ Wir erleben täglich, unter welchem Druck die berufliche Bildung steht: Fachkräftemangel, Transformation der Wirtschaft, Digitalisierung und KI, Integration und zunehmend heterogene Klassen. Diese Aufgaben kann niemand allein lösen. Der jakobb bringt Lehrkräfte, Schulleitungen, Wirtschaft, Verwaltung und Wissenschaft an einen Tisch. Genau diesen Austausch über Zuständigkeiten hinweg brauchen wir jetzt. Gleichzeitig zeigt der jakobb, was die beruflichen Schulen in Baden-Württemberg leisten. Sie sind kein Plan B, sondern ein Erfolgsmodell und das Rückgrat der Fachkräftesicherung im Land.“

Der jakobb bringt die Akteure der beruflichen Bildung miteinander ins Gespräch. (Foto © Laurenz Bostedt für Klett MEX)

**Raus aus dem Tagungsraum, rein in die Praxis**

Ein weiteres Alleinstellungsmerkmal des Kongresses ist die konsequente Verbindung von Theorie und Praxis: Wenn die Fachvorträge und Diskussionsrunden enden, öffnen regelmäßig am zweiten Veranstaltungstag Spitzenunternehmen sowie innovative berufsbildende Schulen in der Region Stuttgart ihre Türen für exklusive „jakobb-Führungen“. **Dr. Benny Pock**, Geschäftsführer von Klett MEX und Mitgründer des jakobb, unterstreicht die Bedeutung dieses Formats: „ Der jakobb belässt es nicht beim theoretischen Diskurs. Unser Ziel war von Anfang an, die beiden Lernorte der dualen Ausbildung – den betrieblichen und den schulischen Teil – nicht nur an einen Tisch zu bringen, sondern vor Ort erlebbar zu machen. Die Exkursionen bieten Ausbildungsverantwortlichen und Lehrkräften die Chance, voneinander zu lernen, Best Practices im laufenden Betrieb zu studieren und frische Impulse direkt in die eigene Ausbildungspraxis mitzunehmen.“

…

items.body:
# How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes

- How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes – The Marginalian ABOUT CONTACT SUPPORT SUBSCRIBE Newsletter RSS CONNECT Facebook Twitter Instagram Tumblr How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes By Maria Popova Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable , that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage. Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop , the golden fan of the gingko , the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe . In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is. Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive. Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.” What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”). A taste: What do we say to longing? If you have sat in the chill of early morning bleakness and watched as the deep blue sighed and blushed, touched by the warm curve of dawn and pinker than pink then apricot soft and spreading its glow, you know. You know. How — in this dim parade of brutality — might all be well? But if we trouble it with light, train our sights on the rebellious good, and work to make it truer. Beneath the face of the water, wonder. In dark woods, a gate. In the chapter called lostness, a friend. All the help we could not yet see. It cannot be always comfortable. So love the thousand knives as they enter and see your shape still sitting. See that you too belong to paws of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled roots, to silver-spun constellations. Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us. The big secret is this: No one else can brave you. Messy, yes. And marvelous. What is more than we see in this world we’re pressed into, its blistered barking noise? For what we build, speak, and ruin — our efforts, our angers. For music. For wings. — Published November 25, 2026 — https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/25/rachel-hebert-thanks/ — www.themarginalian.org PRINT ARTICLE EMAIL ARTICLE Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook

items.body:
An old Victorian infirmary transformed into an [educational space](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/education-tag/) by UK studio [Bennetts Associates](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/bennetts-associates/) has won the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland for 2026.

Named the Edinburgh Futures Institute, the project involved refurbishing the Category A-listed structure, originally designed by Scottish architect David Bryce, and integrating new teaching and work spaces for the University of Edinburgh.

The [Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/royal-incorporation-of-architects-in-scotland/) (RIAS) said the award jury praised the project for its “modern, welcoming, clever and stimulating” design that successfully blends “Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation”.

Photo by Keith Hunter

“The Edinburgh Futures Institute stood out for its civic generosity, scale and ambition," said [RIAS](https://www.rias.org.uk/) president Libby Heathcote, who is associate director at [Reiach and Hall Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/reiach-and-hall-architects/).

“Balancing loyalty to David Bryce’s diagram with creativity in introducing bold new interventions is a remarkable achievement, blending historic Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation," she continued.

“The result is a modern, welcoming, clever, and stimulating place that people want to work in and return to."

Photo by Peter Cook

Central to [Bennetts Associates](https://www.bennettsassociates.com/)' redevelopment was the restoration of the building’s existing fabric, which was at risk of dereliction after being vacated in 2003.

Updates to the existing structure included reopening an original clock tower and public plaza, as well as the restoration of original wards and 150-metre-long corridors.

Across its five floors, flexible teaching and work zones were added alongside new public areas such as exhibition space and a 450-seat event hall below ground.

Photo by Hufton and Crow

The Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual prize named after Scottish architect Andrew Doolan, who passed away in 2004. It recognises buildings of all typologies.

The Edinburgh Futures Institute was chosen as this year’s winner ahead of two other adaptive reuse projects. These have each been featured in a series of videos produced by [Jim Stephenson](https://clickclickjim.com/) and published by Dezeen and RIAS to showcase the shortlist.

[Read: Studio Octopi revives art deco pavilion and lido on Scottish coast](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/13/tarlair-outdoor-pool-pavilion-studio-octopi-andrew-doolan-award/)

The other two projects shortlisted were the [Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by London-based Studio Octopi](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/13/tarlair-outdoor-pool-pavilion-studio-octopi-andrew-doolan-award/) and the [Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/06/collective-architecture-paisley-central-library-rias-doolan-award/).

Previous winners of the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland award include the [Union Terrace Gardens by Stallan-Brand and LDA Design](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/12/05/union-terrace-gardens-rias-andrew-doolan/) and the [Burrell Collection museum by John McAslan + Partners](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/11/22/burrell-collection-andrew-doolan-best-building/).

items.subtitle: – Weird and in person celebrations of books.

items.body:
– Weird and in person celebrations of books.

– Listening to a poem while doing my little stretches. The [Library of Congress](https://www.loc.gov/programs/poetry-and-literature/audio-recordings/archive-of-recorded-poetry-and-literature/) and [Poetry Archive](https://poetryarchive.org/about-us/) collections, to be specific.

– And I’m thankful in advance to the programmer who builds me a little widget or website that streams a random poem from these archives.

– The [new Marlon James](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780593717202). I’m late to the party, but damn.

– Finding something cool in a pile of books someone is giving away.

– The major book awards no longer being afraid of support for Palestine, and [Paradiso 17](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780593804056) and *[Huna](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9798217153602)* winning NBAs.

– A really good pen. I’ve had two instances recently where I had a small bookstore coupon that I spent on luxe pens. Highly recommend treating yourself to a fine writing instrument.

– [Funny novels with funny first person narrators.](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9781609450618)

– The tide continuing to turn against AI. I’m thankful we may see AI’s high water mark very soon.

– Getting to interview Adam Peterson for the release of [his story collection.](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780814259986)

– Booksellers, who are in the middle of their most hectic season. I’m thankful for everyone who treats them reasonably this time of year.

– Peanuts, a Perfect Snack For Reading.

– Librarians, who are always in the middle of hectic season.

– [Flaming Hydra](https://flaminghydra.com/), and especially Luke O’Neil’s recent [New England Week](https://flaminghydra.com/new-england-week/) which I’m revisiting as I pack up to go to Boston for the holiday.

– Connecting with a stranger over a book, especially that thing where someone points at your book from a distance, and you close it and hold up the cover, and they give you a thumbs up. Really good stuff.

– Small presses, and all the cool and weird things they’re taking a chance on.

– [Marilynne Robinson](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9781250784018). Her middle name is Summers, but she’s an autumn writer.

– My sweet seven month old showing preferences for books. And I also chew on the books that I like, so I’m thankful that he inherited that trait from me.

– Trying to explain [Gene Wolfe](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9781250781253)’s deal to someone for the first time.

– A [small](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780984469345) [book](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9781836744429) you can read in an afternoon. Also having an afternoon free to read.

– [Olga Ravn’s gift guide](https://olgaravn.substack.com/p/a-gift-guide-from-your-slightly-esoteric?publication_id=5907042&post_id=226504999&isFreemail=true&r=bsaw&triedRedirect=true), which includes Ibuprofen and haunted dolls.

– Reading an author who is really going for it and trying something new. I appreciate someone taking a risk, regardless of the outcome. (Usually.)

– A friend asking for a book recommendation, and then actually reading your recommendation, and then telling you they liked your recommendation. No better feeling in the world.

items.body:
# „Stark unter Druck“ – Leitfaden zum Umgang mit Belastungen im Redaktionsalltag

Zeitdruck, knappe Ressourcen, belastende Recherchethemen und öffentliche Anfeindungen können journalistische Arbeit erschweren. Auch für redaktionell arbeitende Teams in der Wissenschaftskommunikation stellt sich deshalb die Frage, wie sich Belastungen frühzeitig erkennen und reduzieren lassen. Der Leitfaden „Stark unter Druck – Was Redaktionen gegen Überlastung tun können“ setzt bei den unterschiedlichen Handlungsmöglichkeiten von Mitarbeitenden, Führungskräften und Medienhäusern an. Dabei nimmt er auch strukturelle Ursachen von Überlastung in den Blick.

Die Publikation von Netzwerk Recherche beruht auf Gesprächen mit 90 redaktionellen Führungskräften, Betriebsrät*innen und Personalverantwortlichen. Aus diesen Gesprächen wurden die Erfahrungen und erprobten Ansätze in diesem Leitfaden zusammengetragen. Die Empfehlung sind nach Verantwortungsebenen geordnet, sodass Leser*innen gezielt Anregungen für den eigenen Arbeitsbereich finden können.

Für Redaktionsmitglieder und Freie geht es etwa darum, Grenzen zu setzen, Arbeitsanforderungen zu klären und Kolleg*innen Unterstützung anzubieten. Ein Beispiel sind freiwillige Check-ins von Besprechungen: Kurze Gesprächsrunden können sichtbar machen, wer gerade besonders belastet ist und Hilfe benötigt. Führungskräfte erhalten Impulse, um Austausch im Team zu ermöglichen, mit Hassrede umzugehen und freie Mitarbeitende in Unterstützungsangebote einzubeziehen. Auf Ebene des oberen Managements stehen unter anderem Coaching, betriebliche Gesundheitsangebote und die Begleitung organisatorischer Veränderungen im Mittelpunkt. Angaben zu Kosten und Zeitaufwand helfen dabei, die Umsetzung einzuschätzen.

Welche Maßnahmen passen zum eigenen Team? Der Leitfaden versteht sich als Baukasten, aus dem Redaktionen geeignete Ansätze auswählen und weiterentwickeln können. Viele Vorschläge sind bewusst niederschwellig angelegt. Zugleich weisen die Autor*innen darauf hin, dass nicht jede Idee in jedem Arbeitsumfeld funktioniert.

Für den Wissenschaftsjournalismus/die Wissenschaftskommunikation bietet die Publikation vor allem Anregungen zur Gestaltung redaktioneller Zusammenarbeit. Klare Erwartungen, realistische Arbeitsziele und verlässliche Unterstützung können Redaktionen und auch in Kommunikationsteams wichtige Ansatzpunkte sein. Der Leitfaden regt dazu an, Belastungen offen anzusprechen und gemeinsam zu prüfen, welche Veränderungen im eigenen Einflussbereich liegen und wo Entscheidungen der Leitung erforderlich sind.

- Journalist*innen
- Öffentlichkeitsarbeitende

items.body:
The home page of Salon’s website in November 1999.

In the dying days of 1995, I was a freelance journalist in Portland, Oregon, who spent most of my time seated at a rickety particle-board desk, a gift from my father-in-law. The desk was covered in faux-walnut laminate and swayed from side to side as I wrote. I had already finished my main financial gusher for that year, a history book for fifth graders, and I needed more work.

In this respect I was no different than any freelancer in literary history. In fact, the technology involved in my trade, and the speed at which it functioned—its industrial metabolism—had hardly changed in the preceding century. Of course, I had a computer. But it hardly seemed to be much more than a glorified typewriter. And of course I had an email account, courtesy of the nerd Valhalla known as CompuServe. But the business of freelance journalism was still built largely around stuffing wads of paper into envelopes and sending them to editors, who would then transform the contents into other wads of paper: newspapers, magazines, books. The product, whatever you thought of it, was palpable.

Into this cozy Victorian setting came an online publication called Salon. It had been launched that same fall by a crew of ex-staffers from the San Francisco Examiner, traditional journalists trying to break the mold. I don’t remember which Salon editor contacted me in the first place. I do remember reading the website in my chilly little office, steadying the stupid desk with one leg and feeling an almost metaphysical puzzlement. Salon wasn’t some programmer’s hobby, whipped up in creaky old COBOL. It looked like a magazine, with zippy graphics and respectable fonts. The prose was smart, stylish, and amusingly contrarian.

All of this made a kind of sense to me. What was tricky was that it was free. That first afternoon, I printed out one of the articles, about The Beatles Anthology, which was just then airing on TV. I suppose I was turning back the technological clock—transubstantiating the product back into paper. Reading Salon gratis made me feel as if I were doing something furtive, as though I were a shoplifter, but it represented a kind of post-Gutenberg freedom.

Over the next year, I would write many pieces for Salon. I started out with book reviews that were assigned to me by Dwight Garner. (He had previously edited a few things of mine at Vogue, in terms of ethos the absolute inverse of Salon and, eventually, in terms of finances too.) Dwight sent me books by the bushel, or so it felt. I wrote very short pieces for him very quickly; they appeared online almost immediately. This, for the journalist, was unprecedented and nearly beggared belief. No more waiting for your piece to come out, pacing the equivalent of a widow’s walk. Sometimes I was even instructed to send the piece straight to the copy editor so we could cut a few more minutes out of the process.

Speediness of reflexes was part of the value proposition for Salon. Within months, the “smart tabloid,” as its founder David Talbot called it, was posting daily rather than weekly. In this way it inaugurated a fire-hose style of journalism that would in time become universal. The new norm was not waiting, not allowing stories to lose their heat in the cooling saucer of classic media.

Salon’s politics were similarly nontraditional: left-leaning, libertarian-adjacent (as per its Bay Area digs), but without an obvious party line. It doubtless helped that the magazine was not a subsidiary of a larger corporation, which was the case with Slate (part of Microsoft) and the earlier, cruder Mr. Showbiz (part of Starwave, a short-lived multimedia platform founded by Microsoft’s Paul Allen). Yes, Salon’s seed funding had come from Apple—a mingy $60,000—followed by a more substantial disbursement to the tune of $2 million from the Adobe cofounder John Warnock and various other investors. But it was an independent entity, unconstrained by the need to tiptoe around the feelings of a corporate proprietor.

…

items.title: I Don’t Like Your Tone
items.subtitle: When the pressure to make everything perfect leaves us feeling irritable and overwhelmed, mindfulness can help us find our way back to connection.
items.feedText: Does this sound familiar? You’ve decided to host a gathering and spent far more time and money on it than you expected. Because you really wanted to extend yourself, but now you are just a little more frazzled than you wanted to be. But you ignore your difficult feelings and press on. Or maybe everything has lined up perfectly for your event and then one of your guests arrives and tells you that they forgot to mention that they don’t eat gluten, dairy, meat, beans, fiber, or sugar and now you feel totally unprepared. Or maybe a well-meaning family member says something they think is funny, and you find it hurtful and it makes you want to close down.
items.body:
# I Don’t Like Your Tone

Does this sound familiar? You’ve decided to host a gathering and spent far more time and money on it than you expected. But that’s OK. Because you really wanted to extend yourself, but now you are just a little more frazzled than you wanted to be. But you ignore your difficult feelings and press on.

Or maybe everything has lined up perfectly for your event and then one of your guests arrives and tells you that they forgot to mention that they don’t eat gluten, dairy, meat, beans, fiber, or sugar and now you feel totally unprepared. Or maybe a well-meaning family member says something they think is funny, and you find it hurtful and it makes you want to close down.

Suddenly your perfect event is going sideways and you find yourself looking for a crawlspace to hide in or someone to snap at. These are the moments when mindfulness can help us pause, take a breath, and acknowledge that things aren’t going as planned. Rather than getting swept up in frustration, we can reconnect with our original intention: bringing people together in a welcoming, loving atmosphere.

Social gatherings can give us a rich and wonderful opportunity to strengthen bonds of love and connection. But even the best-laid plans can quickly turn into emotional meltdowns unless we make a point of pausing to recognize when we get caught up in the impossible task of trying to get everything right.

Instead, you can plan a new kind of to-do list. One that puts self-care and the creation of a loving atmosphere as the top priority.

I am usually the person in my family who hosts the celebrations. Yet every year, I seem to get amnesia about how tired, overwhelmed, and irritated I feel by the time the first person gets there.

I go the extra mile to make an overflowing amount of hand crafted food. I take time to create a charming atmosphere. But by the time my guests arrive, I have barely slept in a week and have long forgotten why I wanted to bring everyone together in the first place. Somewhere along the way, my self-imposed expectations had taken over. Instead of being the warm, welcoming host I’d hoped to be, I became the anxious, overburdened kitchen help, desperately trying to keep the food train going.

During a particularly big event when I really tried to outdo myself, a close friend and two family members told me I seemed uptight and terse. And, as if that weren’t enough, they didn’t like my tone!

“You don’t like my TONE? What? How dare you! Ungrateful clods.”

After skulking away in a state of icy fury, my years of mindfulness practice eventually kicked in and a few hundred breaths later I managed to notice how I had lost sight of my heartfelt intention of creating a welcoming haven for love and connection.

Instead, I’d become so focused on getting everything done that I’d turned the gathering into a military operation.

I regularly remind myself how valuable it is when I take a moment to be curious, rather than certain. When I could finally get there, my investigations helped me notice that my shoulders were up and I was holding my breath.

I could feel the tightness in my face every time someone interrupted me with their warm hellos. I could recognize that somewhere along the way, I had lost sight of my true desire to help nourish joy for myself and everyone else.

Expecting ourselves to regulate our emotions perfectly in the middle of a difficult moment is asking a lot.

I needed some space and time to process what had happened before I could do anything other than snap at someone or run away.

Although I was too reactive in the moment to appreciate the honest feedback about my tone, once I had time to step back and reflect, I could recognize and accept, without having to like it, that my tone was sharp, and not in keeping with my intention for the event.

At the same time, looking more closely at my reactions helped me see how worn out I was feeling and that I really needed to offer myself wisdom and self-care.

So what can mindfulness offer us in moments like these?

## Born Erased ~ What You Destroy, I Love

Born Erased brings together two sides of Bulgarian musician Angel Simitchiev’s musical practice: the dark ambient experimentation of his former solo project Mytrip and the harsher sounds of Dayin, which he once described as “Harsh drones and regret. But it’s a relief.” His third outing as Born Erased, What You Destroy, I Love , revisits the concrete angst of his 2023 debut, I Am the End of the World , with a heavier emphasis on guitars and live percussion. There’s even a touch of colour, at least in Silvana Ilieva’s artwork, which resembles molten lava flowing beneath the earth’s surface.

Simitchiev, however, offers no soothing remedy for the world’s ailments. Written in response to the seemingly endless cycle of wars, human suffering and environmental destruction, the album is an expression of anger at humanity’s willingness to sacrifice life and the natural world in pursuit of power and profit. The opening “Knife Hands” establishes the mood with crushing drones that ebb and flow beneath skies already blackened by an unrelenting darkness, like ink rapidly spreading across watercolour paper. “Sea of Skin” begins with a low rumble from the earth’s core before erupting into post-rock territory, propelled by drums and distorted guitars.

As Simitchiev explains in the accompanying interview, the compositions began as ambient pieces, with drummer Nedislav Miladinov invited to respond freely to their atmosphere. Only afterwards did Simitchiev write the guitar and bass parts around the recorded drums. This approach accounts for some of the music’s unpredictable momentum, as the pieces expand and contract under their own considerable weight.

On “Diamond Silence”, the magmatic force reaches the surface, accompanied by the ghostly vocals of Romain Barbot of Saåad, whose fragile presence offers a rare moment of intimacy. “Like Wraiths” takes us across scorched earth, while “The Last Embrace” moves through coruscating textures, with Siavash Amini contributing additional layers of noise and disquiet.

“Unbelonging” retreats into more familiar dark ambient territory, its steady drumming offering a deceptive sense of reassurance as sweeping, glacial drones clear the horizon of any remaining sonic debris. The piece eventually erupts into a volcanic torrent of distortion, dispelling any illusion of safety. It’s this false familiarity that makes the album so unsettling: just when the music seems to offer some respite, the ground gives way again.

The closing “A Future Without the Body” abandons all hope of salvation. Its thrusting, strident passages seem intent on stripping away the last remnants of humanity before gradually dissipating into thin air. The silence left in their wake is all the more powerful.

What You Destroy, I Love offers little prospect of redemption. Simitchiev’s anger is directed not at the natural world but at humanity’s determination to destroy it, along with itself. If there is any hope remaining, it lies in the possibility that the planet might eventually reclaim what we have so recklessly squandered.

Born Erased live by Niya Kirkova

To uncover the different layers of the production process I have reached out directly to Angel Simitchiev .

What You Destroy, I Love sounds considerably heavier than Birds Drink My Blood , with elements of shoegaze and post-rock. In some ways, it feels closer to your debut, I Am the End of the World , which drew on your background in hardcore punk. Was this a conscious return to that sound? And how much did Nedislav Miladinov’s drumming influence the direction of the album?

…

## FLORIAN LÓPEZ constructs TWO-MODULE PLAY INSTALLATION

Designed by Florian López, Alchemy is an **[interactive free-play installation](https://www.designboom.com/tag/interactive-installation/)**for children and adults that organizes an**[exhibition](https://www.designboom.com/tag/exhibition-design/)**space as an anatomical body to be traversed. The structure comprises two architectural modules linked by tubular conduits and clad on the exterior in**[timber](https://www.designboom.com/tag/wood-and-timber-architecture/)** treated with the Japanese yakisugi charring technique, creating a blackened, fissured surface that functions as a protective outer skin. Circular openings cut into the charred facades act as physical thresholds into a three-stage interior sequence.

Alchemy is a free-play installation for children and adults | all images ©Dylan Perrenoud

## YAKISUGI-CHARRED WOOD clads Alchemy PLAY INSTALLATION

The first module begins in darkness, housing black inflatable volumes shaped after intestinal forms and kept in continuous motion by a steady airflow to create a soft, enveloping environment. From there, visitors pass into a six-sided mirrored chamber that multiplies reflections across all surfaces, shifting perspective and spatial awareness.

Crossing into the second module, **[the designer](http://florianlopez.ch)** shifts the interior from individual perception to collaborative assembly. Lined with pink recycled rebonded foam referencing internal flesh and muscle tissue, the room is stocked with loose geometric blocks without prescriptive instructions, inviting children and adults to negotiate and build shared structures through open-ended play.

items.title: Mindful Eating
items.subtitle: This food reveals your connection with the Earth.
items.feedText: With mindfulness we can see that many elements—the rain, sunshine, earth, and the labor of the farmers, drivers, food sellers, and cook—have all come together to form each wonderful meal. When we eat in mindfulness, we can see that the entire universe is supporting our existence. Having the opportunity to sit and enjoy a wonderful meal is something precious, something not everyone has. Many people in the world are hungry. When I hold a bowl of rice or a piece of bread, I know that I am fortunate, and I feel comp…
items.body:
Mindful eating is an important part of our meditation practice—from chopping vegetables to eating with awareness to cleaning up. With [mindfulness](http://google.com/url?q=https://tricycle.org/buddhism-misunderstandings/%23mindfulness-primary-practice&sa=D&source=editors&ust=1794344459664192&usg=AOvVaw3noZmbxwjn3sqon9r8wjed) we can see that many elements—the rain, sunshine, earth, and the labor of the farmers, drivers, food sellers, and cook—have all come together to form each wonderful meal. When we eat in mindfulness, we can see that the entire universe is supporting our existence.

Having the opportunity to sit and enjoy a wonderful meal is something precious, something not everyone has. Many people in the world are hungry. When I hold a bowl of rice or a piece of bread, I know that I am fortunate, and I feel [compassion](https://tricycle.org/tag/compassion-karuna/) for all those who have no food to eat or who are without friends or family. We can be aware of this right at our dinner table. Mindful eating can cultivate seeds of compassion and understanding. Those seeds can sprout and grow inside us and give us the determination to do something to help hungry and lonely people to be nourished.

The kitchen should be a place of meditation. You might want to create a kitchen altar to remind yourself to practice mindfulness while cooking. It can be just a small shelf with enough room for an incense holder, a small flower vase, a beautiful stone, a small picture of an ancestor or a spiritual teacher, or a statue of the Buddha or a [bodhisattva](https://tricycle.org/glossary/bodhisattva/)—whatever is most meaningful to you. When you come into the kitchen, you can begin your work by offering incense and practicing mindful breathing.

While cooking, allow enough time so you don’t feel rushed. Be aware that you, and the people you’re cooking for, depend on this food. This awareness will help you to cook healthy food that’s infused with your love and mindfulness.

When the food is on the table and everyone is seated, practice at least three mindful breaths before beginning to eat. You can say:

*Breathing in, I calm my body.* *Breathing out, I smile.*

If you’re eating alone, promise yourself just to eat and to be with the food, and not to read or listen to the radio or watch a screen during the meal. If you’re eating with others, take the time to really look at each of them and smile. Sitting at the table with other people is a chance to offer an authentic smile of friendship and understanding. It’s very easy, but not many people do it. To me, the most important part of the practice is to look at each person and smile. If people eating together cannot smile at each other, then something isn’t right.

After breathing and smiling, look down at the food in a way that allows it to become real. This food reveals your connection with the Earth. Each bite contains the life of the sun and the Earth. The extent to which your food reveals itself depends on you. You can see and taste the whole universe in a piece of bread!

Contemplating your food for a few seconds before eating, and eating in mindfulness, can bring you much happiness. You can say:

*In this food* *I see clearly the presence* *of the entire universe* *supporting my existence.*

When you’ve finished eating, take a few moments to notice that your bowl or plate is now empty and your hunger is satisfied. You can take a moment to be grateful that you have had this nourishing food to eat, supporting you on the path of love and understanding, by saying:

*The plate is empty.* *My hunger is satisfied.* *I vow to live* *for the benefit of all beings.*

When you’re cleaning the kitchen or [washing dishes](https://tricycle.org/magazine/wash-your-bowl/), do it as if you were washing a baby, and you can feel joy and peace radiate within and around you. You can say to yourself:

*Washing the dishes* *is like bathing a baby.* *The profane is the sacred.* *Everyday mind is enlightened mind.*

…

## Das XEN FX Delay auf dem iPad

Anfang November ist das Liquid Sky d-vices Zen FX Lab als Plugin erschienen. Dabei handelt es sich um den Nachfolger der Zen Delay Software. Jetzt hat sich Liquid Sky d-vices dazu entschieden, das Effekt Plugin auch für das iPad herauszubringen.

## Gibt es Unterschiede zwischen der iPad Version und der PC-Version?

Die Funktionen unterscheiden sich nicht von der Plugin-Version. Allerdings lässt sich das Zen FX Lab jetzt über den Touchscreen des iPads bedienen und als AUv3 Plugin in iPad DAWs einbinden.

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit für die iPad Version

**Zum Einführungspreis ist Zen FX Lab für 9,99 Euro im [Apple App Store](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/xen-fx-lab/id6815805463)erhältlich. Nach der Einführungsphase wird der Preis auf 17,99 Euro steigen.**

## Das XEN FX Delay

Xen FX Lab ist die überarbeitete Version des Zen Delay Virtual und dieses basiert auf dem Zen Delay. Das Plugin kombiniert Delay, Filter und Spring Reverb mit umfangreichen Modulationsmöglichkeiten und richtet sich an alle, die mehr als klassische Echoeffekte suchen. Die neue Version bringt zusätzliche Funktionen und eröffnet Möglichkeiten für ungewöhnliches und kreatives Sounddesign.

Im Folgenden konzentriere ich mich auf die Neuerungen von XEN FX DELAY. Wer über genauere Details informiert werden möchte, kann sich folgende Tests durchlesen:

[Hier geht es zum Test des Zen Delay Virtual](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/erica-synths-zen-delay-virtual-test/)

[Hier geht es zum Test der Zen Delay Hardware.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/ninja-tune-zen-delay-test/)

## Was kann das XEN FX DELAY?

Die Umbenennung in Xen FX Lab war ein guter Schritt. Denn bei diesem Plugin handelt es sich um weit mehr als ein einfaches Delay. Es ist eine richtig fette Sounddesign Maschine, mit der man wirklich ungewöhnliche klangliche Ergebnisse erzielen kann, die weit über das hinausgehen, was ein reguläres Delay schafft. Dabei helfen die unglaublichen vielfältigen Modulationsmöglichkeiten für das Delay, das Filter und das neu hinzugekommene Spring Reverb.

## Die Neuerungen: Das Hauptmenü

Auffällig ist das UFO Logo in der Mitte der Software, an dessen Stelle sich früher die Röhre befand. Links und rechts davon finden sich nun zwei Slider, mit denen sich die verschiedenen Delay-Zeiten und Filtertypen einstellen lassen.

Ansonsten hat sich am Layout nicht viel geändert. Links befindet sich wie gewohnt die Einstellung für das Delay. Rechts sind die Filter und Drive Sektion sowie ein Regler zur Anpassung des Eingangssignals untergebracht.

Xen FX Lab Hauptmenü Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Das Spring Reverb

Neu ist das Spring Reverb, das über einen ausgeprägt metallischen Charakter verfügt. Für die Klanggestaltung stehen die Parameter Mix, Tension, Tone, Decay und Regen zur Verfügung. Damit lassen sich typische Spring-Reverb-Effekte erzeugen, aber auch extreme Klangwelten erschaffen. Manchmal klingt es so, als befände man sich in einem riesigen Tanklaster oder in einem ausgehöhlten Todesstern aus Star Wars. Einfach verrückt.

Xen FX Lab Presets (Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Die Dub Funktion

Besonders interessant ist die neue Dub Funktion. Mit einem Knopfdruck lassen sich die Delay, Filter und Spring Reverb Effekte ein und ausschalten. So kann man dem trockenen Signal gezielt zusätzliche Effekte hinzufügen. Jeder Parameter von Xen FX Lab lässt sich automatisieren. Auch die Dub Funktion kann automatisiert und per MIDI angesteuert werden. Dadurch lassen sich Delays taktgenau und punktuell zum trockenen Signal hinzumischen.

…

items.subtitle: What if our cities were designed to help us slow down, take in the world around us, and connect with the people we encounter every day?

items.body:
# Awe-Makers: Designing Cities for Connection

### Transcript

Scroll down for a transcription of this episode.

What if our cities were designed to help us slow down, take in the world around us, and connect with the people we encounter every day? Social anthropologist and urban designer Louise Vogel Kielgast shares how thoughtful public spaces can make room for more awe and human connection in everyday life.

Summary: The places we live shape how we feel, connect, and experience the world around us. In our new Awe-Makers series, we meet the people reimagining public spaces that make public life thrive. We begin with social anthropologist and urban designer Louise Vogel Kielgast, who shares how thoughtful city design can create more opportunities for awe, from welcoming public spaces and urban nature to everyday encounters with strangers. She explores how putting people, especially children, at the center of urban planning can help build communities where everyone has more room to wonder and connect.

How To Do This Practice:

- Slow down and look around: The next time you're walking, biking, or commuting, take a moment to move at a slower pace. Notice what's happening around you rather than focusing only on where you're going.
- Explore a shared space: Visit a neighborhood park, farmers market, public garden, waterfront, or town square. Look for places that invite you to pause, explore, and spend time with others.
- Notice the small wonders: Pay attention to details you might normally overlook, like a beautiful tree, a piece of public art, the sound of music, or an unexpected interaction between strangers.
- Make room for connection: Smile at someone, make eye contact, or strike up a brief conversation. Even small moments of social connection can help us feel more connected to our communities.
- See your surroundings through a child's eyes: Notice what might spark a child's curiosity, from an interesting texture to a bird in a tree. Let yourself approach the world with that same sense of openness and discovery.
- Think about how your community could inspire awe: What would make your neighborhood more welcoming, beautiful, or connected? Consider how you might contribute, whether by supporting a community garden, attending a local event, or advocating for more inviting public spaces.
Today’s Guest:

LOUISE VOGEL KIELGAST is a social anthropologist and urban designer.

Learn more about the Cities of Awe initiative and join a growing community of awe makers by visiting www.citiesofawe.com .

items.body:
# SynthMaker Adds Classic ICs As Circuit Components, With Playable Atari Punk Console

ViDesk Ltd has added classic integrated circuits as playable components in SynthMaker , its browser-based circuit simulator and music software.

The new parts let users build and hear circuits using logic chips, 555 timers, classic synthesizer ICs and audio-processing chips, with each component modeled from its datasheet.

The additions include logic gates, flip-flops, counters and switches, along with the 555 timer. Examples include a ring modulator built with a 4070, a sub-octave circuit using a 4013, a Baby 8 sequencer based on a 4017 and a six-voice drone using a 40106. Synthesizer IC models include the 2164 VCA, 3340 oscillator, 3320 and 2140 filters, and 4046 phase-locked loop.

The update also adds audio and delay chips, including a 3207 bucket-brigade chorus, PT2399 echo, LM386 amplifier and LM311 comparator. Circuits are entered by part number, with pin connections following the manufacturer’s datasheet, then simulated part by part so users can hear the result and change component values.

To demonstrate the new components, SynthMaker has added a playable Atari Punk Console page. The two-knob stepped-tone circuit uses the two halves of a 556 dual timer, with Pitch and Step controls, and includes an interactive schematic and parts list. Visitors can play it in a browser without installing the software.

Sounds created with the new chip models can also be exported as instruments for the SynthMaker Player plugin. The Player supports VST3 and CLAP, plus Audio Units on macOS, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. The SynthMaker Manual adds three pages of example circuits covering logic and timer chips, synthesizer ICs, and delay, amplifier and comparator chips.

Features:

- Classic logic ICs, including gates, flip-flops, counters and switches
- 555 timer and 556 dual-timer support
- 4070, 4013, 4017 and 40106 logic-chip models
- 2164 VCA, 3340 oscillator, 3320 and 2140 filters, and 4046 PLL models
- 3207 bucket-brigade chorus, PT2399 echo, LM386 amplifier and LM311 comparator models
- ICs entered by part number with pin connections based on manufacturer datasheets
- Part-by-part circuit simulation with audio playback
- Interactive Atari Punk Console page with Pitch and Step controls, schematic and parts list
- Export of chip-based sounds as instruments for the SynthMaker Player plugin
- Player support for VST3 and CLAP, plus Audio Unit on macOS
- Browser-based version and desktop apps for macOS, Windows and Linux
- Three new Manual pages with playable example circuits
Pricing & Availability:

The new chip models and Atari Punk Console demo are available to play for free in SynthMaker ; creating and editing custom circuits requires the one-time-purchase SynthMaker Pro edition. SynthMaker is available in a web browser and as desktop apps for macOS, Windows and Linux.

items.feedText: These settings face significant challenges in delivering effective support, such as shortages of mental health specialists, long waiting times, and overcrowding. items.body: Background: Emergency departments play a central role in crisis management for children and young people’s (CYP) mental health. These settings face significant challenges in delivering effective support, such as shortages of mental health specialists, long waiting times, and overcrowding. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may have the potential to expand access to care, bridge service gaps, and alleviate pressure on emergency settings for CYP experiencing mental health crises. Objective: This review systematically reviews the current evidence for the acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness of DMHIs for CYP in emergency care settings. Methods: We conducted database searches using APA PsycInfo, Embase, MEDLINE, and Web of Science from January 2015 to September 2025. We included quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods studies that related to the acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness of DMHIs in acute settings. Acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility were added as post hoc outcomes for this secondary review after implementation-related evidence was identified in the original search. DMHIs included telepsychiatry, phone calls, SMS text messaging, and computerized interventions. In addition to studies reporting data from CYP under the age of 25 years, we included those evaluating data from caregivers and care providers. All selected studies were assessed for quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results: Overall, 6778 articles were retrieved from the database searches, of which 13 articles met the inclusion criteria. In total, data from 1495 patients, of whom 1048 received a DMHI, 413 caregivers, and 250 care providers were included across studies, excluding 1 study that did not report the sample size for care providers. Mental health presentations included depressive symptoms, violent behaviors, suicidal ideation and attempts, intoxication, and multiple mental health conditions. DMHIs were broadly acceptable, particularly for interventions such as telepsychiatry and structured follow-up phone calls. Feasibility, appropriateness, and cost-effectiveness outcomes were more varied. These were affected by the specific intervention design, emergency care context, and user characteristics. CYP valued computerized interventions that incorporated age-appropriate design and language; telepsychiatry, phone calls, and automated SMS text messaging interventions that enabled continued support and connectedness with health care professionals; and interventions delivered at appropriate intervals. Conversely, health care providers raised concerns about increasing workloads for interventions that required specialist facilitation. Electronic cognitive behavioral therapy was viewed as more appropriate for CYP with prior therapy experience, and SMS text messaging intervention outcomes were limited in CYP with histories of behavioral violence. Conclusions: DMHIs show promise in supporting the mental health care needs of CYP in emergency care settings. CYP, caregivers, and care providers demonstrated a willingness to use these tools, but careful consideration is needed to improve the appropriateness and feasibility of these interventions. More diverse studies are needed to explore these findings in different contexts and to address existing shortcomings to support the implementation of DMHIs.

items.body:
## Town Comes Together To Guide Child’s Medevac Plane After Runway Lights Broke

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/igiugig-alaska-runway-medevac-plane/)

The remote village of Igiugig, Alaska, has given the world a masterclass in solidarity. Even more impressive, they did so despite only having a population of about 70 people. When a medical evacuation team couldn’t land at the local airport to help a child because the runway lights were broken, the city showed up, lining up their cars to guide the plane with their headlights.

It all started when Ida Nelson, head tribal clerk based in this small southwest Alaska village, heard a loud noise after 11:30 PM on August 28, 2020. “When they first flew over, I was like ’oh my gosh,’ that sounds like a weird vehicle. I’ve never heard that truck before. And it wasn’t a truck, it was an airplane,” Nelson told [KTOO](https://www.ktoo.org/2020/08/29/the-runway-lights-broke-but-igiugig-guided-in-a-childs-medevac-plane-with-headlights/). “Anytime there’s any type of planes flying after dark, you always assume it’s going to be something urgent and an emergency.”

And it was an emergency: a LifeMed Alaska crew was trying to land. When Nelson, who lives close to the airport, looked outside, she realized the runway lights weren't working. Worried, she got in her truck, where she met a local pilot who had also noticed the issue. While pilots can usually turn runway lights from their aircraft, that didn’t work this time. Nelson and the pilot also tried turning on the lights manually from the ground to no avail.

Concerned, Nelson offered to light up one end of the runway with her truck, but they still needed more help. And so, Nelson’s neighbor rallied the community, making 32 phone calls. Meanwhile, the pilot hopped into his own plane and contacted the LifeMed crew. “I was feeling nervous, anxious because this is late at night and this is someone’s child,” Nelson told[CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/2020/09/01/us/alaska-village-medical-evacuation-trnd). “The only thing I could think of was how quickly I could get other people here to help because what if that was my baby’s plane?”

Within 20 minutes, 20 people had shown up in their vehicles, many in their pajamas, ready to follow the plane crew’s instructions. The townspeople staggered their cars and 4-wheelers along the runway so the pilot could see end to end. The people remained in place as the plane landed, boarded the patient, and departed safely for Anchorage, where the young patient made it to the hospital in stable condition.

While the LifeMed Alaska crew are no strangers to harsh Alaskan conditions, they were impressed by the community’s efforts to help one of their own. The team took one photo of the Igiugig runway lit up by its residents as they took off, and shared it on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CEmfI8aBGng/) with the message, “It’s amazing what a community can accomplish with a little ingenuity and a lot of determination!”

items.body: IntroductionMultimodal physiological approaches can characterize complementary aspects of emotional processing that are not available from a single signal.MethodsWe analyzed synchronized high-density EEG and eye-tracking recordings from a publicly available developmental dataset of children and adolescents younger than 18 years who viewed negative, neutral, and positive naturalistic videos. The SPRiNT algorithm provided time-resolved aperiodic EEG Exponent and Offset estimates, and their dependence with pupil diameter was quantified using mutual information (MI) and correlation-based coupling metrics within labeled scalp sensor groups.ResultsIn the original analysis, Friedman tests showed a consistent condition effect for both Offset-pupil and Exponent-pupil MI across all six scalp groups (Kendall's W = 0.762 − 0.830, all pFDR<10-7). Pairwise tests showed greater MI during the negative video than during the neutral or positive videos (standardized r = 0.869 − 0.874, all pFDR<10-7), whereas no neutral-positive MI difference was detected.DiscussionBy integrating cortical spectral dynamics with a peripheral measure of arousal and attention, this approach provides a framework for studying brain-autonomic coordination during naturalistic emotional processing in children and adolescents.

items.body:
# CRSSD Festival Announces Lineup For Spring 2027 Edition

News » CRSSD Festival Announces Lineup For Spring 2027 Edition CRSSD Festival Announces Lineup For Spring 2027 Edition Share Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Returning to San Diego’s Waterfront Park on 13 and 14 March 2027, CRSSD Festival has opened presale access for its spring edition. CRSSD returns to Waterfront Park in San Diego on 13 and 14 March 2027. The line-up includes Boris Brejcha, Drumcode founder Adam Beyer, a back-to-back set from Ellen Allien and Marcel Dettmann, and Doncaster’s Mella Dee. Joseph Capriati, Dennis Cruz, Indira Paganotto and Disco Lines are also on the bill.

It will be one of Brejcha’s last festival sets. In October, the German producer announced that 2027 will be his final year playing festivals, after which he plans to close the chapter on Boris Brejcha and the Joker, the masked persona he has performed as since 2006.

### Berlin techno and the UK contingent

Allien and Dettmann have both been part of Berlin techno for decades. Allien founded the BPitch label in 1999, and Dettmann has long been associated with Berghain. Beyer, who launched Drumcode in 1996, is joined on the techno side of the bill by Maceo Plex, Portuguese artist ØTTA and Berlin trance duo DJ Heartstring.

Mella Dee, fresh of his latest release Changes, heads a sizeable UK contingent. The Doncaster producer, who runs the Warehouse Music label, is joined by Josh Baker, Max Dean, Gaskin and Joss Dean. SOSA and Julian Fijma b2b ALISHA represent the deeper end of house.

Further down the bill, Anish Kumar plays back-to-back with Peruvian producer Sofia Kourtesis. Attack featured the British producer in 2022, and this booking is the latest sign that his rise has continued.

The full line-up also includes Eric Prydz, Sven Väth, Luciano, DJ Hell and Dubfire b2b Nicole Moudaber. Noga Erez, Kasablanca, Toro y Moi and Digitalism, who play live, bring a crossover element.

### CRSSD After Dark & CRSSD Lab

Waterfront Park again hosts three stages (Ocean View, City Steps and The Palms), and CRSSD Lab returns with its vinyl market. CRSSD After Dark carries the weekend on into San Diego’s clubs; that programme is still to be announced.

- Alumni presale: Tuesday 1 December 2026, 12 noon PT, for Weekend Pass holders from listed past editions. Single-day and third-party tickets, including Tixel, are not eligible.
- Community presale: Wednesday 2 December 2026, 12 noon PT, for fans who sign up in advance.
- General sale: Wednesday 2 December 2026, 2 pm PT.

items.body:
[Open video on YouTube ↗](https://youtu.be/qjPcaZf_plo?si=jlK6QKTo3kmWidgv&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

[Clay](https://www.clay.com/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use.

Jeff joined Clay when it [acquired Avenue](https://clay.com/blog/avenue?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay [raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation](https://www.clay.com/blog/series-d?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv).

Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute.

### Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent.

When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings.

The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows.

Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together.

[Jump to the Sculptor discussion →](https://youtu.be/qjPcaZf_plo?t=1125&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### Most companies post-train too early

For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks.

Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million.

[Jump to the post-training discussion →](https://youtu.be/qjPcaZf_plo?t=1668&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

### $1,500 to score every company in the world

Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market.

## The Contents of Perception

In contemporary philosophy, the phrase ’the contents of perception’ means, roughly, what is conveyed to the subject by her perceptual experience. For example, suppose you are looking into a piano at the array of hammers and strings. There will be a way these things look to you when you see them: they will look to have a certain shape, color, texture, and arrangement relative to one another, among other things. Your visual experience conveys to you that the piano has these features. If your experience is illusory in some respect then the piano won’t really have all those features. But even then, there will still be something conveyed to you by your experience. Three main questions will be addressed in this entry. First (Sections 1–2), what are contents and what is their relation to experiences? Second (Sections 3–7), which contents are contents of experience? Finally (Section 8), in virtue of what do experiences have contents, when they do?

## 1. What are Perceptual Experiences?

This entry will focus exclusively on the contents of perceptual experiences . It is definitional of experience, as the term is used here, that they have some phenomenal character, or more briefly, some phenomenology. The phenomenology of an experience is what it is like for the subject to have it. At any given waking moment, one normally has experiences in some (perhaps all) of the five sense modalities, along with proprioceptive experience of some sort. Like occurrent emotions and background moods, these contribute to one’s overall experience . Each of five sense modalities seems to be accompanied by a distinctive kind of phenomenology. Sometimes the boundaries between them can be hard to draw, for example between olfactory and gustatory phenomenology, kinesthetic experience and haptic-tactile experience (that is, tactile experiences involving movement rather than just pressure sensation), and perhaps, in some cases, between the latter two and visual experience (on the last point see Press et al . 2004, Kennett et al . 2001, Fotopoulou et al . 2009; on distinguishing the senses, see Stokes, Matthen and Briggs 2014, Wilson and Macpherson 2018). In general, it is an open question how holistic perceptual experiences, and to what extent it can be viewed as an aggregate of separable experiences in distinct modalities. Despite these difficulties, some rough distinctions can be drawn: the difference between seeing red and seeing blue is not a difference in how things sound, or in how one’s body feels.

items.title: South Korea proceeds with case over allegedly misleading Apple Intelligence ads
items.subtitle: South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) announced today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intell…
items.feedText: South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) announced today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup. Here are the details. Back in March 2025, shortly after Apple announced it was delaying the rollout of what would eventually become Siri AI, the South Korean civic group Seoul YMCA filed a complaint with the KFTC. At the time, Yonhap reported that the organization had previously called on Apple to compensate affected customers, and alleged that the company may have continued to market the iPhone 16 lineup despite already knowing that some of its advertised AI features would be delayed. As 9to5Mac readers will likely remember, Apple widely advertised Apple Intelligence and AI-powered Siri features as part of its iPhone 16 launch campaign, going so far as to give its iconic Fifth Avenue store an Apple Intelligence-themed makeover and run an ad campaign starring Bella Ramsey. This landed Apple in legal and regulatory trouble in multiple markets, including the US, where the company agreed to a $250 million class action settlement earlier this year, and Brazil , where it came under scrutiny from a consumer protection agency in May.

# South Korea proceeds with case over allegedly misleading Apple Intelligence ads - 9to5Mac

- AAPL Company
- Apple Intelligence
- South Korea
## South Korea proceeds with case over allegedly misleading Apple Intelligence ads

South Korea’s Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) announced today that it has opened formal proceedings against Apple over its advertising of Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup. Here are the details.

## A bit of background

Back in March 2025, shortly after Apple announced it was delaying the rollout of what would eventually become Siri AI, the South Korean civic group Seoul YMCA filed a complaint with the KFTC.

At the time, Yonhap reported that the organization had previously called on Apple to compensate affected customers, and alleged that the company may have continued to market the iPhone 16 lineup despite already knowing that some of its advertised AI features would be delayed.

As 9to5Mac readers will likely remember, Apple widely advertised Apple Intelligence and AI-powered Siri features as part of its iPhone 16 launch campaign, going so far as to give its iconic Fifth Avenue store an Apple Intelligence-themed makeover and run an ad campaign starring Bella Ramsey.

This landed Apple in legal and regulatory trouble in multiple markets, including the US, where the company agreed to a $250 million class action settlement earlier this year, and Brazil , where it came under scrutiny from a consumer protection agency in May. Now, the company is facing potential penalties in South Korea as well.

## Apple faces potential penalties in South Korea

As a result of Seoul YMCA’s complaint, the KFTC conducted an investigation into Apple’s advertising practices. Today, the regulator announced (via MacRumors ) that its investigators had submitted their findings and recommendations for formal deliberation by the Commission.

According to the KFTC’s press release, investigators concluded that Apple advertised Apple Intelligence and its planned staggered rollout on the iPhone 16 website, but “concealed, downplayed, or omitted information material to consumers’ purchasing decisions.”

That included, per the press release (translation ours):

> The fact that some of the nine Apple Intelligence features would be difficult to deliver in US English by the end of 2024, and when those features would become available. The fact that some features were not available in US English as of October 2024. The fact that some features would be difficult to deliver in Korean by early April 2025, and when those features would become available.

The press release also notes that Genmoji, Image Playground, “Siri with the ability to understand personal context,” and “Siri that provides step-by-step guidance” were not made available as advertised:

> For example, Siri’s ability to understand personal context was advertised as being scheduled to launch first in US English by the end of 2024, as currently available in US English in October 2024, and as scheduled to support Korean in early April 2025. In reality, the feature was not launched in US English until September 2026, with Korean language support following in October 2026.

As a result, the investigators concluded that Apple’s conduct constituted a violation of the country’s Labeling and Advertising Act, which prohibits deceptive labeling and advertising.

They recommended issuing corrective orders, including a prohibition on such conduct in the future, as well as imposing a financial penalty.

They also estimate that Apple’s revenue associated with the alleged violation amounts to approximately 3.35 trillion South Korean won (roughly $2.5 billion), though the KFTC’s press release does not specify the amount of the fine.

⁠ Yonhap noted today that the fine could reach roughly $48 million, while ⁠ KBS reported that it could range between $21 million and $42 million.

With the report now submitted, Apple has six weeks to submit its written defense before the Commission deliberates and makes a final determination on whether the company violated the law and, if so, how much it should be fined.

# Merz verkündet vorzeitiges Ende des EU-Sondergipfels

Haushaltsberatungen in Brüssel Merz verkündet vorzeitiges Ende des EU-Sondergipfels Stand: 27.11.2026 • 01:02 Uhr

Die Vorstellungen unter den 27 Staats- und Regierungschefs lagen weit auseinander. So weit, dass sie laut Merz den zweiten angesetzten Tag des Gipfels ausfallen lassen. Es geht um viele Milliarden für den EU-Haushalt.

Noch vor dem offiziellen Ende des Gipfels sind der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz vor die Presse getreten. Es werde keinen Abschluss mehr geben, verkündete Merz in Brüssel. Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der 27 Mitgliedstaaten waren zusammengekommen, um den nächsten EU-Haushalt zu beraten. Doch nun das vorzeitige Ende.

Merz setze dennoch weiter auf einen Abschluss über den mittelfristigen Finanzrahmen (MFR) noch in diesem Jahr. Nur werde eine Einigung auf dem Sondergipfel nicht mehr gelingen. Deshalb würden die 27 EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs auf den zweiten Gipfeltag am Freitag verzichten.

Ursprünglich waren zwei Tage eingeplant gewesen. Andere Länder sehen deshalb den Gipfel schon als gescheitert an. Es geht um viel Geld. Der letzte Vorschlag lag bei rund 1.700 Milliarden Euro. So viel will die EU in den Jahren zwischen 2028 bis 2034 ausgeben für Landwirtschaft, Wirtschaftsförderung, Verteidigung und Regionales. Doch das ist den Deutschen zu viel. Bundeskanzler Merz verlangt noch einige 100 Milliarden Euro weniger. Doch es gibt keine Einigung, wo gespart werden soll.

26.11.2026

### Haushaltsgipfel in Brüssel Merz fordert weitere Kürzung der EU-Finanzen

Den jüngsten Kompromiss lehnt der Bundeskanzler ab. Er knüpft seine Zustimmung außerdem weiter an die Ukraine-Hilfe. mehr

## Merz gegen neue Schulden

Merz schloss neue Schulden auf europäischer Ebene aus. "Auf dem nächsten mittelfristigen Finanzrahmen werden Zinsen von über 150 Milliarden Euro in diesen sieben Jahren lasten", warnte er. "Das ist sehr viel, und deswegen dürfen wir uns auch nicht weiter verschulden. Wir verlieren sonst unsere Handlungsfähigkeit."

Kurz vor dem offiziellen Beginn des Gipfels hatte sich Merz mit ähnlich gesinnten Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus den Nettozahler-Staaten Niederlande, Österreich, Schweden, Finnland, Dänemark und Belgien getroffen. Die Gruppe nennt sich seit dem jüngsten Dazustoßen Belgiens "Die vernünftigen Sieben". Damit will sie deutlich machen, dass ein zu großer EU-Haushalt aus ihrer Sicht unvernünftig wäre.

26.11.2026

### EU-Haushalt Kampf um bis zu zwei Billionen Euro

Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der 27 EU-Länder beraten in Brüssel über den langfristigen EU-Haushalt. mehr

## Meloni: "Lichtjahre" von Einigung entfernt

Ihnen gegenüber steht eine große Gruppe von Ländern, die keine weiteren Kürzungen wollen und hohe EU-Ausgaben für strukturschwache Regionen und die Landwirtschaft verteidigen. Viele dieser Staaten, vor allem in Süd- und Osteuropa, sind Nettoempfänger aus dem EU-Haushalt.

Kritik kommt zudem von Ländern wie Frankreich und Italien, die auch Nettozahler sind, aber Einbußen für ihre Landwirte und Regionen vermeiden wollen. "Wir sind nicht bereit, unsere Unterschrift unter ein Budget zu setzen, in das wir mehr einzahlen, um weniger zu bekommen", machte Italiens Regierungschefin Giorgia Meloni klar. Man sei noch "Lichtjahre" von einer Einigung entfernt.

## Weiter geht es im Dezember

EU-Ratspräsident António Costa hatte im sogenannten Beichtstuhlverfahren versucht, die Differenzen zwischen den sehr unterschiedlichen Lagern zu verkleinern. Doch trotz der vertraulichen Gespräche mit einzelnen Interessengruppen zur Auslotung der Kompromissbereitschaft gibt es zunächst keine erkennbare Bewegung in der festgefahrenen Patt-Situation.

Der französische Präsident Macron hat bei einem der größten Posten, den Agrarausgaben, kein Entgegenkommen gezeigt. Im Dezember werden die Staats- und Regierungschefs einen weiteren Versuch starten. Weihnachten wollen wir alle zu Hause sein, so die optimistische Prognose des Kanzlers.

Mit Informationen von Sabrina Fritz, ARD-Studio Brüssel .
