items.body:
One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million) at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

Legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “ *jatte-téton* ” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape.

Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek *mastos*, or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized *jatte-tétons* delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.

The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer acquired the piece, which is known to have once belonged to the French Marquise de Chanaleilles.

“Jatte-téton” and its tripod from the Rambouillet dairy, 1787, hard-paste porcelain, h. 12 cm,” porcelain Manufacture Royale de Sèvres.

Three of the four breast bowls made in 1787 and 1788 for the queen’s royal dairy dishes are housed in public collections today, including two at the Musée de Sèvres and one at the Museo Duca di Martina in Naples. The bowl that sold tonight is the last of that specific series. They are “the most celebrated and the most extravagant shape of the porcelain service,” by the royal Sèvres manufactory for the queen’s dairy, notes the auction house in its description.

With the bowl comes an intricately carved tripod stand decorated with goat heads in relief, as seen above. Indeed, the breast bowls require a pedestal to hold them upside down, as it were, so as to contain the milk and cream they were meant to serve.

Speaking to *[Le Journal des Arts](https://www.lejournaldesarts.fr/marche/le-dernier-bol-sein-de-marie-antoinette-reapparait-186736)* about the bowl, auctioneer Alexandre de La Forest Divonne observed: “It has become something of a symbol of the queen; it is truly a totem.”

# SnipNotes 7: Komplett neu entwickelt, Mac-App zieht mit iOS gleich

## SnipNotes 7: Komplett neu entwickelt, Mac-App zieht mit iOS gleich

von Carsten Knobloch 26. Nov. 2026 | 0

SnipNotes ist in Version 7 erschienen. Die App selbst begleite ich schon seit vielen Jahren. Auch wenn ich sie nicht nutze, beobachte ich sie natürlich - wie viele Apps für meine Berichterstattung. Was mir zuerst aufgefallen ist: die Mac-App. Die wirkt jetzt echt besser, sodass ich mal in einer ruhigen Stunde noch genauer reinschauen werde (bin ja meistens Team Werks-Apps, sprich: Apple Notizen).

Der Entwickler hat die App von Grund auf neu geschrieben, die Daten wandern beim ersten Start automatisch ins neue Format. Notizen, Kategorien, Anhänge und unterstützte Einstellungen bleiben also erhalten. Je nach Größe der Sammlung dauert die Übernahme etwas, die App sollte man in dieser Zeit nicht weiter nutzen.

Voraussetzung ist iOS 26, iPadOS 26 oder macOS 26. Die bisherige Version lief noch ab iOS 15 und macOS 12. Wer ältere Geräte nutzt, bleibt dort bei der alten App-Version, die Notizen werden weiterhin per iCloud mit Geräten synchronisiert, auf denen SnipNotes 7 läuft. Nur neue Funktionen wie Notizverknüpfungen gibt es dort nicht.

### Notizen verknüpfen und Rückverweise

Mit die größte Neuerung laut Felix, dem Entwickler: Ihr könnt Notizen miteinander verlinken und per Tippen oder Klicken zwischen ihnen springen. Das lässt sich etwa für eine Projektübersicht mit einzelnen Aufgaben, Besprechungsnotizen samt Dokumenten oder Reisenotizen mit Zielen, Reservierungen und Packlisten nutzen. Dazu kommen Rückverweise: In einer Notiz seht ihr direkt, welche anderen Notizen auf sie verlinken. Links zu externen Webseiten bleiben kostenlos. Notizverknüpfungen und Rückverweise gibt es dagegen als separaten Einmalkauf, sie sind aber in den SnipNotes-Plus-Abonnements und bestimmten bereits erworbenen Gesamtpaketen enthalten.

### Privatsphäre und Organisation

Bisher ließ sich die ganze App oder eine Kategorie per Code schützen, jetzt könnt ihr auch einzelne Notizen sperren. Geöffnet werden sie erst nach erfolgreicher Authentifizierung, auf unterstützten Geräten per Face ID oder Touch ID. Den Passwortschutz gibt es nun auch auf dem Mac.

Sortierung und Darstellung der Notizliste lassen sich pro Kategorie festlegen, etwa die zuletzt bearbeiteten Notizen zuerst in der einen, alphabetisch in der anderen. Neu ist außerdem eine Obergrenze für Notizen im Eingang. Ist sie erreicht, können ältere Notizen automatisch in eine andere Kategorie wandern.

### Bearbeitung und Notizaktionen

Fett, Kursiv und Hervorhebungen lassen sich jetzt kombinieren, und Formatierungen funktionieren auch in Notiztiteln. Aktionen für erkannte Inhalte wie Adressen, Telefonnummern oder Links erscheinen als Schaltflächen unter der Notiz und zusätzlich im Kontextmenü der Notizliste. Welche Aktionen beim Wischen über eine Notiz auftauchen, bestimmt ihr selbst, inklusive Reihenfolge. Die Rückgängig-Funktion macht mehrere Bearbeitungsschritte nacheinander rückgängig. Notizen behalten außerdem ihr gewähltes Symbol, erkannte Inhaltstypen werden durch kleinere Zusatzsymbole angezeigt.

### Mac-App auf iOS-Niveau

Die Mac-Version bekommt nun den Funktionsumfang der iOS-App. Neu sind Erinnerungen, Passwortschutz (auf kompatiblen Macs mit Touch ID), Zeichnungen in Notizen und Notizaktionen, etwa um Adressen in Karten zu öffnen, Nummern anzurufen oder Webseiten aufzurufen. Dazu kommen eine bessere Bildvorschau mit Blättern und Zoom sowie Widgets auf dem Schreibtisch und in der Mitteilungszentrale. Alles andere könnt ihr euch selbst durchlesen .

items.body:
# Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance — LessWrong

- Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance — LessWrong x AI Curated 121 Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance by cousin_it 23rd Nov 2026 1 min read 39 121 A very simple point that I've had to explain to many people, so I thought I'd make a post on it. Some classes of people in the past were economically necessary for their labor, but militarily irrelevant and coercible: slaves, serfs. Others didn't do any economic work, but were militarily important: the aristocracy! Living fun lives, partying, traveling, making and enjoying art. Some of them felt a bit of ennui due to not working, but mostly it wasn't a big problem. The reason aristocracy gave way to democracy wasn't because of rising productivity of the masses: a slave in a diamond mine can be very productive, but still remain a slave. Rather, it was because firearms lowered the cost of training a soldier, and thus made the masses valuable as potential soldiers . That gave the masses a bargaining chip which led to better economic and political standing. If Alice wishes for a world where her labor (e.g. as a programmer) remains economically valuable, but all military jobs go to AI, then humans will lose the "potential soldier bonus" we've had for a couple centuries and revert to a powerless, exploited position. The economic importance of our labor won't save us. Whereas if Bob wishes for a world where all jobs in the economy are done by AI, but humans remain militarily important, then humans will be the aristocracy in that world and lead lives of leisure and fun. If I could magically make that future happen, I would. Of course it's all academic: all military jobs can probably be done by AI even sooner than other jobs. There's already surveillance and drones. But still I wanted to write it up, because so many people today think economic irrelevance is the main issue, when it isn't. Sure, in the extreme case where group A has perfect military power, they can use that to extract ~all wealth from group B, even if group B otherwise would have had economic relevance. We might wind up in this situation as a result of improvements in AI, although I think it's more likely that unfriendly superintelligence doesn't need civilian or military labor from humans. In practice, in human history so far, all military power has been less-than-absolute, which means that if group B has significant economic power but no military power, then group B still has some leverage, because attempting to coerce group B to serve you by threats of violence is at least a partially negative-sum transaction. Group B won't work quite as hard or as skillfully under military occupation as they would if they were instead voluntarily trading with you. This is part of why, e.g., workers today in the United Kingdom still earn above subsistence wages even though they mostly don't carry firearms and mostly aren't allowed to. It's also a major theme of, e.g., the Cold War. West Germans had ~no military ability to resist NATO, and East Germans had ~no military ability to resist the Soviet Union; after all, both halves of Germany had just been thoroughly defeated in World War II.

# Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return

- Entertainment
- Streaming
- Netflix
## Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return

A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.

A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.

The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming , and even games . It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner .

If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories .

What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.

But once Midnight Diner ’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.

And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.

But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner ’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

- Andrew Webster

items.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
items.subtitle: Lobsters AI & Machine Learning • Lobsters AI
items.feedText: This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions. My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal. I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant.
items.body:
# To save software engineering from LLMs, we need a mainstream verifiable language

- To save software engineering from LLMs, we need a mainstream verifiable language The culture of software engineering has to change, and that will take many different projects to achieve. published: June 21, 2026 - last updated: July 24, 2026 Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving , and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window) . The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed. Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window) , but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window) . The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window) , all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest. But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering. It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future: It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems.
- Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it.
- Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to even know the right things are being proven . In the words of Leonardo de Moura (opens new window) : Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.
This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.

## § The long winding road of Magmide

My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.

I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window) :

items.body:
# Taking Email Back » Linux Magazine

- How New Open Source Mail Servers and Clients Make Self-Hosting Practical Again The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software. Taking Email Back Photo by Chris G. on Unsplash Author(s): Jeffrey A. McGuire The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software. Three Homes, No Data Center Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way. The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and plans to move to Aerogramme around January 2027. The collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains. Email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence. Two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services. The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development. How Email Got Away from Us In the 1990s, running your own mail server was ordinary. Universities and small companies did it, and so did Mauro De Gennaro. In 1993, as a teenager, he fetched mail for users of his bulletin board over UUCP: the dial-up protocol Unix machines used to exchange mail. He has worked on mail software for most of the three decades since. When he looked at the open source stack again about six years ago, he saw "it's the same software that companies and servers have been using for over 20 years." He counts 12 separate programs to run a conventional self-hosted setup. Each has its own configuration format and logs, written by different people in different styles.

items.title: Astronomers Discover a Hidden Binary in a Star System Used to Calibrate the JWST
items.subtitle: Researchers from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have discovered a binary system in a field used to calibrate the JWST's optics.
items.feedText: Researchers from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have discovered a binary system in a field used to calibrate the JWST's optics.
items.body:
# Astronomers Discover a Hidden Binary in a Star System Used to Calibrate the JWST

When observatories like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) conduct observation campaigns, they often start by observing star fields to calibrate their instruments. These stars must have precisely characterized spectra so that their radiant energy (or fluxes) can be measured accurately. However, some stars that appear as single objects have a binary companion that has not been resolved, altering their predicted stellar flux. In fact, a star that is used for JWST calibration (HD 158485), which was thought to be an A-type star, has been identified as a binary system .

The discovery was made by a team from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), who found the binary while reviewing long-term observations from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , provides the first orbital solution and dynamical mass ratio for the system. HD 158485 is an example of a pulsating, variable, or Delta (δ) Scuti star, which experiences brightness changes at a regular frequency (typically every 18 minutes to 8 hours)

From the TESS data, the team noticed that HD 158485 was pulsing in six distinct rhythms, otherwise known as δ Scuti pulsation modes. They further noticed that these pulses fell into two groups with opposing light-travel-time variations, meaning that the light from these pulses reached Earth at different times. This could only be explained by the presence of a binary companion. The team used the variation between the two signals to trace the star's orbital motion with HD 158485, which showed that they orbit each other every 382.8 days.

Pulsation timing results for HD 158485. The two groups of pulsation modes show opposite time delays, revealing the orbital motion of both stars. Credit: Chenglong, LV et al. (2026).

The data also allowed them to constrain the orbital parameters and the star's mass. According to their calculations, the companion has an eccentricity of 0.242, indicating a moderately elongated, closed elliptical orbit, and is about 80% as massive as its primary - making it a likely F-type (yellow-white) main-sequence star. Their findings are independently confirmed by an orbital model built from earlier TESS data, which accurately predicted the timing variations that were detected by a separate observation campaign.

The team further compared a two-star atmosphere model with a conventional single-star model using the system's mass ratio, which showed a flux difference of about 1.6% between one and five micrometers (μm), and 2.5% between five and 28 μm. These findings could have significant implications where JWST calibration is concerned. While they do not represent a measured error, they do show how mistaking a binary system for a single star can shift predicted fluxes, thus throwing off readings.

In essence, the team's results show that stellar pulsations can reveal binaries that conventional observations leave unresolved. It also underscores the need to account for hidden stellar companions when evaluating calibration standards for our instruments.

Further Reading: Chinese Academy of Sciences

### Matthew Williams

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website .

items.body:
# SAP: IT-Sicherheitsvorfall bei SAP – „Haben verdächtige Aktivitäten identifiziert“

Serverraum: Nach Handelsblatt-Informationen betrifft der IT-Sicherheitsvorfall bei SAP die Softwareentwicklung. (Symbolbild) Foto: AP Düsseldorf. SAP ist von einem IT-Sicherheitsvorfall betroffen: Der Softwarehersteller hat nach eigenen Angaben „verdächtige Aktivitäten“ identifiziert und Gegenmaßnahmen ergriffen. Nach aktuellem Stand der Untersuchung gebe es keine Hinweise auf einen unbefugten Zugriff auf die Geschäftsdaten von Kunden, teilte der Konzern am Donnerstagabend mit. Zuvor hatte der „Spiegel“ über einen „Hackerangriff“ berichtet.

Details wie den Angriffsweg oder mögliche Täter nannte SAP nicht. Nach Handelsblatt-Informationen aus Konzernkreisen ist die Softwareentwicklung betroffen. Unter dem internen Namen „Project Granite“ veranlasste der Softwarehersteller demnach mehrere Sofortmaßnahmen zum Schutz der Entwicklungsinfrastruktur. Zahlreiche Teams seien davon betroffen.

SAP setzt in der Produktentwicklung die Plattform Github ein, auf der Programmierer Programmcode speichern und gemeinsam bearbeiten können. Der „Spiegel“ berichtete unter Berufung auf einen Insider, dass die Angreifer sogenannte Authentifizierungs-Token, also digitale Zugangsschlüssel von SAP-Mitarbeitern für das Portal erbeutet hätten. Damit könnten sie unter Umständen auf Quellcode zugreifen und ihn verändern.

Nach Handelsblatt-Informationen hat SAP mehrere Gegenmaßnahmen ergriffen. So schränkte der Konzern den Zugriff auf Github ein, stoppte automatisierte Abläufe in der Softwareentwicklung und tauschte Signaturschlüssel aus. Das soll verhindern, dass Angreifer mit bereits erbeuteten Zugangsdaten weiter Zugriff auf Systeme und Quellcode haben.

# Kommunizieren auf Reisen: Whatsapp kündigt E-Sim-Karte an

Nachdem Hinweise auf eine E-Sim-Funktion für Whatsapp aufgetaucht waren, hat das Unternehmen den Dienst jetzt offiziell angekündigt. Demnach soll es künftig möglich sein, über die Messenger - App E-Sim-Karten für die Datenkommunikation zu kaufen und zu installieren.

## Mobiles Internet mit wenigen Klicks

Nutzer:innen auf Reisen müssten sich dadurch nicht erst um eine WLAN -Verbindung oder eine lokale Sim-Karte kümmern. Auch Roaminggebühren sollen dadurch der Vergangenheit angehören. items.body:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.

items.title: HumanFish — Predicting Who Actually Wins a Human Chess Game
items.subtitle: The eval bar on a chess broadcast answers the wrong question.
items.feedText: It tells you what happens if two 3600-Elo engines play perfectly with infinite time. HumanFish is an open hybrid model trained on 550,001 tournament positions (91,720 human 2400–2900 games) combining Stockfish 19, Leela Chess Zero, a grandmaster move predictor (DSC-150M), and live tournament clocks. items.body:
> The eval bar on a chess broadcast answers the wrong question. It tells you what happens if two 3600-Elo engines play perfectly with infinite time. What you actually want to know while watching humans play is: who is going to win from here, how likely is a draw, and why?
> HumanFish is an open hybrid model trained on 550,001 tournament positions (91,720 human 2400–2900 games) combining Stockfish 19, Leela Chess Zero, a grandmaster move predictor ( DSC-150M ), and live tournament clocks. It outputs calibrated White Win / Draw / Black Win odds—and shows the concrete moves behind every disagreement right on the board.

I have long wanted such a thing, here is [the link](https://humanfish.vercel.app/methodology). Built by the well-known [book reviewer Patrick Collison](https://chatgpt.com/s/t_6b088852d0288191be4244b86326777b).

items.body:
# EU-Gipfel: Merz kündigt vorzeitiges Ende der Haushaltsberatungen an

Bild vergrößern Die Präsidentin der Europäischen Kommission, Ursula von der Leyen (r), auf dem EU-Gipfel mit Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU)

Der auf zwei Tage angesetzte EU-Sondergipfel in Brüssel soll überraschend bereits in der Nacht zum Freitag zu Ende gehen. Das kündigte Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz ( CDU ) an. Die Staats- und Regierungschefs würden gegen Mitternacht noch einmal zusammenkommen und den Gipfel anschließend beenden.

»Wir wissen, dass wir heute Abend nicht zu einem Ergebnis kommen«, sagte Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz am Abend in einer Pressekonferenz. Man habe sich darauf verständigt, dass man das Treffen am Freitagvormittag nicht fortsetzen werde.

Bei den Verhandlungen über den künftigen EU-Haushalt gebe es laut Merz neue Bewegung hin zu einer Verringerung des Gesamtvolumens. Schon im Vorfeld hatte sich ein Durchbruch nicht abgezeichnet.

Die sieben sogenannten »sparsamen« Länder bekräftigten nach einem Treffen mit EU-Ratspräsident António Costa auf dem Sondergipfel in Brüssel ihre Position, dass das »Gesamtvolumen« des Budgets für die Jahre von 2028 bis 2034 weiter »angepasst« werden müsse, wie aus deutschen Regierungskreisen verlautete. Der polnische Regierungschef Donald Tusk erklärte unterdessen im Onlinedienst X , ein »billiges Europa« könne sich als »sehr teurer Fehler« erweisen.

### Ukrainehilfe als Voraussetzung

Neben Deutschland gehören Österreich , Dänemark , Schweden , Finnland , Belgien und die Niederlande zur Gruppe der Länder, die sich für eine nur mäßige Erhöhung des künftigen EU-Haushalts im Vergleich zum laufenden Budget einsetzen. Sie fordern zudem das Festhalten an den sogenannten Rabatten, die einige Nettozahlerländer auf ihre Beitragszahlungen erhalten. Eine »nachhaltige und dauerhafte« Finanzierung der Ukraine »durch alle Mitgliedstaaten« sei eine weitere Voraussetzung für diese sieben Länder für einen erfolgreichen Abschluss der Verhandlungen, verlautete aus deutschen Regierungskreisen.

Die Verhandlungen um den Mehrjährigen Finanzrahmen (MFR) für die Jahre 2028 bis 2034 schienen zuletzt festgefahren. Ein Gipfel im Oktober hatte keine Ergebnisse gebracht. Das Sondertreffen am Donnerstag soll nun eine erste Annäherung zwischen den Lagern der »Sparsamen« und der »Freunde der Kohäsion« bringen. Die zweite Gruppe plädiert für einen großen Haushalt, der wie bisher auch den Schwerpunkt auf Agrar- und Regionalförderung legen soll. Ihr gehören unter anderem Italien , Polen und Spanien an.

- Vor den Wahlen in Frankreich und Italien: So ringen Merz, Macron und Meloni um Milliarden für Landwirte 2 Min Zur Merkliste hinzufügen 2 Min Zur Merkliste hinzufügen
- Reise zu CDU-Terminen: Nutzte Merz das Privatflugzeug eines ihm bekannten Sockenherstellers? Von Timo Lehmann und Mayank Sharma 4 Min Zur Merkliste hinzufügen 4 Min Zur Merkliste hinzufügen
- meinung meinung • Umstrittene Militärhilfe für Kyjiw: Der Krieg in der Ukraine kostet die Deutschen viel Geld. Sie fallen zu lassen, wäre noch teurer Der SPIEGEL-Leitartikel von Marina Kormbaki 4 Min Zur Merkliste hinzufügen 4 Min Zur Merkliste hinzufügen
Costa hatte in der vergangenen Woche einen neuen Haushaltsentwurf mit einem Gesamtumfang von rund 1,78 Billionen Euro vorgelegt – rund 204 Milliarden Euro weniger als im Vorschlag der EU-Kommission vom vergangenen Jahr.

items.body:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly [Opportunities Newsletter](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/newsletter/opportunities/).

**[Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + Photo](https://innovateartistgrants.org)** **Featured**
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.**

**[Bryson County Retreat](https://www.brysoncountyretreat.org/)** **Featured**
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**Open Calls**

**[Wildlife Photographer of the Year](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/wildlife-photographer-of-the-year/competition.html)** *(International)*
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
**Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.**

**[Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art](https://responsafoundation.com/2026/10/13/this-memory-competition/)** *(International)*
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for *This Memory,* a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead.
**Deadline: December 4, 2026.**

**[Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab](https://www.moabarts.org/public-art-application)** (Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.**

**[Material Works Art Award 2026](https://pci.jotform.com/form/262185636090156)** *(International)*
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
**Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.**

**[Call for Mail Art](https://www.hivebookarts.org/exhibitions/call-for-mail-art)** *(International)*
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition *love|mark*, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
**Deadline:** **December 15, 2026.**

items.body:
The sight of a spiky sea urchin wandering along the floor of the ocean wearing a hat is quite comical, and even more so when it's a bunch of them (I don't know the collective noun for sea urchins) sped up in a time-lapse. They are all wearing a variety of hats that are really rocks, shells, and other ocean debris. Some wear several of these hats at once. One even carries a shell with a hermit crab living in it! But why do they do that? And how did they learn this new behavior? Even then, how did the trend spread among the herd when they don't have eyes or brains the way we think of those organs?

In this clip from the new BBC nature series *Blue Planet III*, Sir David Attenborough narrates a sea urchin fashion show and explains what benefit this adaptation gives these brainless sea creatures. -via [Born in Space](https://www.borninspace.com/)

items.body:
HANAU. **Wegen familiärer Probleme wollte er der Jugendlichen angeblich «Therapiestunden» geben. Schließlich werden er und sein Opfer laut Anklage vom Hausmeister überrascht: Ein Lehrer aus Hessen muss sich nun wegen Missbrauchs vor Gericht verantworten. Kein Einzelfall: Erst in der vergangenen Woche war ein Gymnasiallehrer aus Thüringen wegen** **sexuellen Missbrauchs einer Schülerin zu einer hohen Gefängnisstrafe verurteilt worden.**

Das Gericht hat zu entscheiden. (Symbolfoto.) Foto: Shutterstock / travelview

Vor dem Landgericht Hanau hat der Prozess gegen einen Lehrer begonnen, der eine Schülerin mehrfach sexuell missbraucht haben soll. In einem Fall wirft die Staatsanwaltschaft ihm sogar vor, die zum Tatzeitpunkt 15-Jährige vergewaltigt haben.

Der verbeamtete Lehrer soll im vergangenen Jahr das Vertrauen der Schülerin zunächst unter dem Vorwand erschlichen haben, ihr wegen familiärer Probleme «Therapiestunden» zu geben. Nach Annäherungen soll es nach Angaben der Staatsanwaltschaft zu Küssen und sexuellen Handlungen gekommen sein. Tatorte seien die Schule, ein Wald und eine Wiese gewesen. Ans Licht kam der Missbrauch laut Anklage, als ein Hausmeister im August vergangenen Jahres den Lehrer und die Schülerin in einer Toilette überraschte.

Über seinen Anwalt räumte der nach eigenen Angaben vom Schuldienst suspendierte 48-Jährige sämtliche Missbrauchsfälle ein, bestritt jedoch die Vergewaltigung. Zum Schutz der Minderjährigen schloss das Gericht vor deren Zeugenvernehmung die Öffentlichkeit aus. Der Prozess soll bis Mitte Dezember fortgesetzt werden.

Zahlreiche Missbrauchsfälle in Schulen haben in den vergangenen Monaten für Schlagzeilen gesorgt – zuletzt die Verurteilung eines Gymnasiallehrers aus Thüringen zu sechs Jahren Haft ([News4teachers berichtete](https://www.news4teachers.de/2026/11/schon-wieder-missbrauch-schon-wieder-muss-ein-gymnasiallehrer-ins-gefaengnis/)). *News4teachers / mit Material der dpa*

> [Grooming: „Herr L. scheint auf Teenager zu stehen“ – warum der Lebensraum Schule Missbrauch begünstigt](https://www.news4teachers.de/2026/07/grooming-herr-l-scheint-auf-teenager-zu-stehen-warum-der-lebensraum-schule-missbrauch-beguenstigt-kommission-sieht-erheblichen-reformbedarf/)

items.body:
# Bachs Weihnachtsoratorium in der Martin-Luther-Kirche - Neustadt-Geflüster

Mit Pauken, Trompeten und „Jauchzet, frohlocket“ beginnt am Sonnabend, 12. Dezember, um 19.30 Uhr das Weihnachtsoratorium von Johann Sebastian Bach in der Martin-Luther-Kirche. Unter der Leitung von Elke Voigt erklingen die ersten drei Kantaten des Werkes. Dresdner Bachchor unter der leitung von Elke Voigt – Foto: Kirchgemeinde Traditionell erklingen die ersten drei Kantaten in der Martin-Luther-Kirche am Sonnabend vor dem dritten Advent. Der Dresdner Bachchor, ein eigens zusammengestellter Jugendchor und die Sinfonietta Dresden gestalten den Konzertabend. Als Solistinnen und Solisten wirken Heidi Maria Taubert (Sopran), Ewa Zeuner (Alt), Jonas Finger (Tenor) und Cornelius Uhle (Bass) mit. An ausgewählten Stellen kann das Publikum in die Choräle einstimmen. Fast 300 Jahre Weihnachtsmusik Johann Sebastian Bach komponierte sein Weihnachtsoratorium 1734 als Leipziger Thomaskantor. Anders als heute üblich, erklangen die sechs Kantaten damals nicht an einem Abend, sondern an sechs verschiedenen Festtagen zwischen Weihnachten und dem Dreikönigstag. Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige --> Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige Anzeige --> Anzeige Die ersten drei Kantaten schrieb Bach für die damals noch üblichen drei Weihnachtsfeiertage. In Rezitativen, Arien, Chören und Chorälen erzählen sie von der Geburt Jesu, der Verkündigung durch die Engel und der Anbetung durch die Hirten. Für das Weihnachtsoratorium griff Bach auch auf eigene weltliche Kompositionen zurück. So stammt die Musik des berühmten Eingangschors „Jauchzet, frohlocket“ aus einer Geburtstagskantate für die sächsische Kurfürstin und polnische Königin Maria Josepha. Ursprünglich sang der Chor dazu „Tönet, ihr Pauken! Erschallet, Trompeten!“. Das Konzert findet in der Martin-Luther-Kirche statt. Foto: Archiv, Anton Launer Heute gehört das Weihnachtsoratorium zu den bekanntesten Werken Bachs und vielerorts fest zum musikalischen Programm der Adventszeit. Für Kinder und Jugendliche unter 18 Jahren ist der Eintritt frei. Kartenvorverkauf im Gemeindebüro am Martin-Luther-Platz 5 zu den Öffnungszeiten und online bei Reservix . items.body:
Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, starting on Thanksgiving Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hippie-bating police officer, by the name of [William “Obie” Obanhein](http://www.nytimes.com/1994/09/14/obituaries/william-j-obanhein-alice-s-restaurant-lawman-69.html), arrested Arlo for littering. (Cultural footnote: Obie previously posed for several Norman Rockwell paintings, including the well-known painting, [“The Runaway,”](http://www.artchive.com/artchive/r/rockwell/rockwell_runaway.jpg) that graced a [1958 cover of](https://web.archive.org/web/20180723115710/https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/2012/05/08/archives/a-fond-farewell-to-an-iconic-policeman.html) *[The Saturday Evening Post](https://web.archive.org/web/20180723115710/https://www.saturdayeveningpost.com/2012/05/08/archives/a-fond-farewell-to-an-iconic-policeman.html)*.) In fairly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a misdemeanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the story isn’t over. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the petty crime ironically becomes a basis for disqualifying him from military service in the Vietnam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bitterness as the song builds into a satirical protest against the war: “I’m sittin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, houses and villages after bein’ a litterbug.” And then we’re back to the cheery chorus again: “You can get anything you want, at Alice’s Restaurant.”

We have featured Guthrie’s classic during past years. But, for this Thanksgiving, we give you the illustrated version.

If you would like to support the mission of Open Culture, consider [making a donation to our site](https://bit.ly/3EBHjtX). It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your [contributions](https://bit.ly/3EBHjtX) will help us continue providing the best free cultural and educational materials to learners everywhere. You can contribute through [PayPal](https://www.openculture.com/help-fund-open-culture), [Patreon](https://bit.ly/3eB2GRB), and Venmo (@openculture). Thanks!

items.body:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate [rose 144% from 2007 to 2020](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls [increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10900-019-00678-x).

As the teenagers brainstormed, [Jasmin Brooks Stephens](https://psychology.berkeley.edu/people/jasmin-brooks-stephens), a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s [Jabali Youth Advocacy](https://www.hcnkids.org/jabali-youth-advocacy) organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

The ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”

## A pathway to hope in the face of racism

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, [suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt57150/2025-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf). Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

It’s easy to talk about [structural racism](https://news.berkeley.edu/2025/08/14/watch-berkeley-scholar-explain-structural-racism/) as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the [Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together [worsened suicide risk for Black young adults](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-01327-001).

items.body:
### “The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth…”

*“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,”* thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on [how to find yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/30/nietzsche-find-yourself-schopenhauer-as-educator/). And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan [so brilliantly satirized](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/10/03/ian-mcewan-nutshell-selfhood/) and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — [is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/25/christof-koch-consciousness-qualia/), completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet **Robert Penn Warren** (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in [Democracy and Poetry](https://www.amazon.com/Democracy-Poetry-Jefferson-lecture-humanities/dp/0674196252/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/democracy-and-poetry/oclc/471794841&referer=brief_results)) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about [power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/22/robert-penn-warren-democracy-and-poetry/).

Robert Penn Warren

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that [“human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/06/18/daniel-gilbert-happiness-future-self/) Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

> In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.

In consonance with my own deep belief in [the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming](https://onbeing.org/programs/maria-popova-cartographer-of-meaning-in-a-digital-age/), Warren adds:

> The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that [“poems are physical sites of discovery and sense-records of our humanity,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/29/the-universe-in-verse/) Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

items.body: Background: The developments in generative AI (GenAI) are expected to have a substantial impact on the field of mental health, including the delivery of clinical services and the role of psychologists. However, there is limited knowledge about how psychologists use and perceive GenAI, including its potential, risks, and effects on the future role of psychologists and professional practice. This includes the competency levels among psychologists and factors associated with the intention to use GenAI within the psychology profession. Objective: This study examined the use of GenAI, self-rated digital and GenAI competencies, behavioral intention to use GenAI, and perceptions of its future impact on professional practice among psychology students, internship psychologists, and licensed psychologists in Sweden. Methods: A national cross-sectional online survey was conducted from January to February 2026 in collaboration with the Swedish Psychological Association. The 36-item survey included closed and open-ended questions, including Likert scale, nominal scale, and multiple-choice items. A total of 1077 respondents, with 64.7% (n=697) being women and with a mean age of 45.5 years (SD 13.7), were included in the analyses. Responses were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods, including hierarchical multiple linear regression, ANOVA, and correlational analysis. items.body:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

…

items.body:
Spanish [lighting](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/lighting-products/) brand [Marset](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/marset/) has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice.

[Marset](https://www.marset.com)'s selection includes the [Gambosa table lamp](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/03/05/gambosa-lamp-mathias-hahn-marset-dezeen-showroom/), created by designer Mathias Hahn to reinterpret the classic shade, stem and base as one smooth, glossy sculpture in steel and opal polycarbonate.

Mathias Hahn's Gambosa lamp has a sculptural form

Gambosa is defined by its elegant composition, with a round-ended body that looks as if precariously balanced. It also features a considered cable design that sweeps down one side of the lamp like a signature.

It is distinguished by its select palette of colours, with combinations of orange, moss grey, black, pale pink and opal that evoke mid-century style combined with contemporary curation.

The Lauro lighting is a reissue from 1973

With the [Lauro collection](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/04/17/lauro-lighting-collection-marset-dezeen-showroom/), Marset has revived a genuine 1970s design classic from its own catalogue, featuring chunky tubes of bent steel.

Created by designers P Aragay and J Pérez Mateo, the Lauro lighting comes in table, floor and wall variants. According to Marset, the range represents the technical achievements of a time when bending steel was a huge challenge.

Ringo lighting is reminiscent of a block of ice suspended in the air

Another of the highlights from Marset is the [Ringo lighting](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/05/06/ringo-lighting-joan-gaspar-marset-dezeen-showroom/), crafted by designer Joan Gaspar from transparent polycarbonate that is rotomoulded, giving it a dimpled texture reminiscent of a melting block of ice.

Available in flush-mounted or pendant styles, the design has a simple cylindrical shape, with scale and materiality bringing fresh life and visual impact.

Domus lighting resembles a house illuminated in the dark

Another of Gaspar's designs is [Domus](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/06/03/domus-joan-gaspar-marset-dezeen-showroom/), an angular bollard-style outdoor light that, through simple gesture, recalls a warmly lit house at night.

The design is available in three heights. Units can be optionally combined to create a sculptural look and the illusion of multiple windows.

Glass shades and glowing bars comprise each light in the Fragile range

Geometric glass volumes, metal detailing and glowing bar-shaped lighting elements meet in the [Fragile collection](https://www.dezeen.com/showroom/fragile-lighting-jaume-ramirez-marset-dezeen-showroom/), designed for the brand by Jaume Ramírez.

The lights come in pendant, wall and table formats, each made up of spherical and conical shades that lend them a playful aesthetic.

Table, wall and pendant lights make up the collection

The roots of the [Marset](https://www.marset.com/en/) brand stretch back to the 1940s, when Francisco "Paco" Marset established a small metal foundry in Barcelona.

His grandchildren Javier and Carlos Marset helped reposition the company as the global design brand it is today when they took over in the 1990s, bringing on board designers such as Gaspar, who is a frequent collaborator.

# Donnerstag, der 26. November 2026: Verdächtiger nach Kirchenbeschädigungen in Psychiatrie und Laubenbrand am Morgen · Leipziger Zeitung

- Der Tag
- Topposts
## Donnerstag, der 26. November 2026: Verdächtiger nach Kirchenbeschädigungen in Psychiatrie und Laubenbrand am Morgen

Ein junger Mann gilt als tatverdächtig hinsichtlich einer Serie an Angriffen auf Häuser und Freikirchen, er sitzt jetzt in der Psychiatrie. Und: Ein Laubenbrand im Möckern rief am Donnerstagmorgen die Feuerwehr und die Polizei auf den Plan, zwei Verdächtige wurden gefasst. Die LZ fasst zusammen, was am Donnerstag, dem 26. November 2026, in Leipzig, Sachsen und darüber hinaus wichtig war.

## Angriffe auf Leipziger Freikirchen und Häuser: 26-Jähriger in psychiatrischer Klinik

Nach einer Serie an Sachbeschädigungen gegen Gebäude in Leipzig, die oft von Evangelisch-Freikirchlichen Gemeinden genutzt werden, steht ein Tatverdächtiger im Visier der Behörden. Wie Staatsanwaltschaft und Polizeidirektion heute mitteilten, geriet ein 26-jähriger Mann in Bezug auf zumindest fünf Taten unter Verdacht. Der Beschuldigte soll zudem bedrohliche und beleidigende Inhalte zu einer Person veröffentlicht sowie Privathäuser attackiert haben.

In den vergangenen Wochen und Monaten war es wiederholt zu Taten nach ähnlichem Muster gekommen. Während der Nachtstunden wurden nach Behördenangaben dabei Türen und Fenster durch Steinwurf geschädigt, Schriftzüge mit teils wirrem Inhalt, aber konkretem Personenbezug angebracht und einmal auch ein Hakenkreuz an eine Wand gesprüht.

Der Tatverdächtige soll nach jetzigem Stand im Zustand einer Schuldunfähigkeit oder zumindest verminderten Steuerungsfähigkeit gehandelt haben. Er selbst stamme wohl aus dem Bereich der betroffenen Gemeinden, in denen er einst verkehrte, weswegen die Ermittler von einem persönlichen Motiv ausgehen. Hinweise auf Terrorismus oder Extremismus gäbe es derzeit nicht. Auf Grundlage eines richterlichen Unterbringungsbefehls sitzt der 26-Jährige nun in einem psychiatrischen Krankenhaus. Die Ermittlungen dauern an.

## Laubenbrand: Polizei fasst zwei Verdächtige

Nach einem morgendlichen Laubenbrand in Leipzig-Möckern wurden zwei Tatverdächtige gefasst. Auch das berichtet heute die Polizeidirektion.

Betroffen war eine Kleingartensparte in der Christoph-Probst-Straße, wo der Vollbrand kurz nach 04:00 Uhr am Donnerstag gemeldet wurde. Die Feuerwehr löschte die Flammen. Im Zuge einer Bereichsfahndung stellte die Polizei im Umfeld zwei Verdächtige. Die 18- und 20-Jährigen wurden vorläufig festgenommen, eine mutmaßliche Verbindung zu dem Brandgeschehen wird geprüft.

Über Verletzte wurde nichts bekannt, auch der Sachschaden steht noch nicht fest. Ermittlungen zur Brandursache laufen.

items.body:
## winding stone roofs follow the movement of water in guizhou

The Huangguoshu Scenic Area in [China](https://www.designboom.com/tag/chinese-architecture/)‘s mountainous Guizhou province welcomes visitors beneath a pair of serpentine [roofs](https://www.designboom.com/tag/rooftop-architecture-and-design/) designed by the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design (CAUPD) and AEPA&TSC. The two Beijing-based practices take their formal cues from the movement of the Baishui River, which runs through the region and feeds a waterfall.

The project comprises two visitor centers at the entrances to the Great Waterfall and Tianxingqiao scenic areas. From above, the architecture appears as a series of dark, sinuous ribbons among densely forested mountains. Much of the enclosed building volume disappears beneath grassy slopes, while the extended rooflines trace the paths of visitors through the landscape.

The project grew out of a need to accommodate increasing numbers of tourists in an area whose entrance facilities had become overwhelmed. During peak season, as many as 50,000 people could arrive at the waterfall site in a single day. For the architects, the organization of these crowds became a starting point for the geometry of the buildings.

two visitor centers weave through the mountainous Huangguoshu Scenic Area | images © Wang Ziling

## designing around pedestrian movement

At the Great Waterfall visitor center, the [design team](https://www.caupd.com/) takes advantage of an existing five-meter difference in elevation between the entrance and exit of the scenic area. The terrain had previously complicated the circulation of tourists and shuttle buses, whose routes converged within a relatively small entrance plaza.

The architects redistribute these journeys vertically. Arriving passengers are dropped off at the lower level, while those returning from the waterfall make their way toward an elevated departure area. Shuttle buses circulate between the two along a one-way route. The arrangement gives each pedestrian journey its own continuous architectural space beneath the sweeping roofs.

Reception and ticketing facilities occupy spaces along these routes, and restaurants have been relocated toward the return journey. These enclosed programs sit largely within the hillside. As visitors approach the waterfall, the most prominent architectural elements are the long, sloping canopies overhead and the stone surfaces that extend along the ground.

the sweeping rooflines take their formal cues from the movement of water

## an elevated journey through the landscape

A similar approach informs the smaller, 1,800-square-meter visitor center at Tianxingqiao, an area known for its natural formations of water and limestone. Here, a four-meter difference in elevation allows the architects to make the roof itself part of the pedestrian circulation system.

While incoming visitors pass through a ground-level hall, those leaving the scenic area walk across the top of the building. An elevated viewing platform offers a place to stop along the return route, with dining facilities that overlook the landscape. Elsewhere, the roof curls upward to shelter the ticketing and waiting areas beneath its extended eaves.

The team retained the site’s mature trees throughout construction and incorporated them into the new architecture. Planted islands punctuate the paved surfaces around the entrance, a landscape composition that draws from the particular arrangement of vegetation and exposed rock within Tianxingqiao.

sinuous canopies organize pedestrian circulation across the entrance plaza

## regional stone houses inform the flowing architecture

For both visitor centers, CAUPD and AEPA&TSC look to the vernacular stone houses of Guizhou. These buildings traditionally feature roofs made from overlapping stone slabs, a construction language that the architects adapt to the much larger scale of the tourism infrastructure.

items.body:
**DÜSSELDORF. Der nordrhein-westfälische Landtag hat ein Verbot von Gesichtsschleiern an Schulen beschlossen. Wie häufig Schülerinnen überhaupt vollverschleiert zum Unterricht erscheinen, ist allerdings selbst dem Schulministerium nicht bekannt. Öffentlich dokumentiert sind nur wenige Einzelfälle – darunter einer, bei dem die Schulleitung bewusst auf ein Verbot verzichtete, weil der Schulfrieden nicht gestört war. Eine Petition, die daraufhin eine Gesetzesänderung forderte, blieb vor zwei Jahren noch erfolglos. Mit der Novelle des Schulgesetzes erhalten Schulleitungen zugleich mehr Möglichkeiten, gegen Gewalt und Bedrohungen durch Schülerinnen und Schüler vorzugehen.**

Problem gelöst, das es in der Praxis nordrhein-westfälischer Schulen gar nicht gibt? (Symbolfoto.) Foto: Shutterstock

Mit den Stimmen der Regierungsfraktionen von CDU und Grünen hat der nordrhein-westfälische Landtag am späten Mittwochabend das „Gesetz zur Stärkung der Bildungsgerechtigkeit und der Demokratiebildung“ beschlossen. Es enthält unter anderem ein Gesichtsverhüllungsverbot für Schülerinnen und Schüler. Dazu heißt es: „Sie dürfen durch ihr Verhalten oder die Verhüllung ihres Gesichts im Unterricht, bei sonstigen schulischen Veranstaltungen und auf dem Schulgelände nicht die Kommunikation erschweren und ihre Mitwirkungspflichten verletzen.“ Ausnahmen sind das Tragen von Atemschutzmasken etwa im Chemieunterricht oder wegen einer Erkrankung.

„Kommunikation ist mehr als die bloße Wahrnehmbarkeit des gesprochenen Wortes“, heißt es im Gesetzentwurf. „Sie setzt auch das Erfassen der Körpersprache, insbesondere der Gesichtsmimik, voraus.“ Schülerinnen und Schüler seien daher verpflichtet, „mit geeigneter Bekleidung am Unterricht teilzunehmen und keine Gesichtsverhüllung zu tragen, die eine Identifizierung und eine Kommunikation erschwert“.

Das Verwaltungsgericht Düsseldorf hatte Ende 2024 im Fall einer 17 Jahre alten Schülerin entschieden, dass ein Berufskolleg ihr die Teilnahme am Unterricht mit einem Gesichtsschleier untersagen durfte – bereits auf Grundlage der bisherigen Rechtslage.

## Schulministerium hat keine belastbaren Zahlen

Wie verbreitet das Phänomen ist, das die Landesregierung mit dem Verbot adressiert, ist allerdings unklar. Dem Schulministerium lägen „keine belastbaren landesweiten Zahlen“ darüber vor, wie häufig Schülerinnen mit einer Gesichtsverschleierung zum Unterricht erscheinen oder dazu gedrängt werden, einen Gesichtsschleier zu tragen, erklärte das Ministerium vergangene Woche [auf Anfrage des WDR](https://www1.wdr.de/politik/politik-in-nrw/gesichtsschleier-in-der-schule-100.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com). Lediglich vereinzelt hätten Schulen den Wunsch nach mehr Rechtssicherheit geäußert. Im Dezember 2017 hatte die Landesregierung auf eine parlamentarische Anfrage der AfD noch mitgeteilt, dass ihr keine entsprechenden Fälle bekannt seien.

Ein weiterer Fall aus dem Jahr 2024, mit dem sich der Petitionsausschuss des Landtags beschäftigte, zeigt, wie unterschiedlich Schulen mit dem Phänomen umgingen. Eine Schülerin war seit Februar mit einem Niqab zum Unterricht erschienen, einem Gesichtsschleier, der lediglich die Augenpartie freilässt. Die Schulleitung hatte in Abstimmung mit der oberen Schulaufsicht entschieden, keine Maßnahmen gegen die Schülerin zu ergreifen. Ihre Identität konnte bei Klausuren von einer weiblichen Lehrkraft überprüft werden. Der Schulfrieden sei nicht beeinträchtigt gewesen, berichtete das Schulministerium laut einem [veröffentlichten Beschluss des Petitionsausschusses](https://www.landtag.nrw.de/portal/WWW/dokumentenarchiv/Dokument/MMPE18-24.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com#page=68). Es habe weder Nachahmerinnen noch missionarische Aktivitäten der Schülerin gegeben. „Es sei weder zu Auseinandersetzungen noch Feindseligkeiten in der Schülerschaft gekommen.“

items.body:
Gloria Steinem was booked up. There had been luncheons and interviews scheduled for the fall; a high-profile conversation with Katie Couric at 92NY and a prominent place in The New Yorker Festival’s lineup. She left appearances unfulfilled, interviews unaired, an essay unpublished and a forthcoming book. In short: Gloria Steinem was, at 92, far from done.

That energy is palpable in that very book, her memoir [An Unexpected Life](https://bookshop.org/p/books/an-unexpected-life-notes-from-a-hope-a-holic-gloria-steinem/4b7ec63a4c7acf42/?aid=132!), published on September 22, in which she states that she planned to live to at least 100. Although she was “older than [she] ever imagined,” mortality didn’t really cross her mind much. Any why would it, when she was also “happier than [she] ever imagined” and her calendar was bursting at the seams? Part memoir, part manifesto, part consciousness raising group, *An Unexpected Life* is a collection of essays in which Steinem reflects on her life, lays out her worldview and looks towards the future. And just as she was in life, on the page she radiates a matter-of-fact conviction and an unflinching clarity—the result of more than sixty years spent organizing a movement.

Her story begins long before she would become the most prominent face of second-wave feminism (although Steinem would reject this label), with a bruised childhood in Toledo, Ohio. She spent stretches of her young life on the road, until her father left when she was ten years old, leaving her in a rat-infested home caring for her increasingly mentally ill mother. With a childhood spent longing for warm kitchens and cookie cutter family units, it is striking that Steinem would grow up to spend so much of her adult life traveling around the country, more often than not living out of a suitcase. But even more formative than her earliest years, perhaps, was the time spent in India in her early 20s, an experience that would become the very foundation of her feminism.

Although mortality was far from Steinem’s mind, it is apparent in these pages that she was hyperaware of her legacy. “At my age, in this still hierarchical time, people often ask me if I’m ‘passing the torch,’” she wrote in her 1983 book [Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellion s](https://bookshop.org/p/books/outrageous-acts-and-everyday-rebellions-third-edition-gloria-steinem/753219586e6d55f1/?aid=132!). “I explain that I’m keeping my torch, thank you very much—and I’m using it to light the torches of others.”

She is doing just that in *An Unexpected Life*, a text bursting with a kind of hopeful exhilaration about what could be. “Nothing is more exciting than making the invisible visible. It’s like finding the end in a ball of yarn,” she wrote. “Pull on it, and gradually the whole of patriarchy unravels.” At times, she gets as literal as bullet-point lists on how to best organize a feminist movement. There are glimmers of the—often cited—shortcomings of the women’s movement that she was at the helm of herself. “Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement,” is one such takeaway of Steinem’s. “Otherwise, people will have a distorted view.” There is an added poignancy to the essays upon her passing; a book that is as much about her life as it is a handbook for movement building. “Whatever my story might be to other people,” Steinem wrote, “I hope something has ripple effects that I myself may never see.”

One such ripple effect concerns her beloved home, an apartment in a brownstone building on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. “If time and ingenuity allow,” Steinem wrote in the book’s prologue, “I hope to acquire the other floors in this house and leave this whole building as a refuge for diverse women who need a place to stay or just to meet.”
